entire-graph · agentic-swebench · rep30

Does the code graph save tokens?

Target was −35% on Sonnet and Haiku, on a 30-instance representative sample. It was not met on either as an aggregate. The reason turns out not to be a configuration that hasn't been found yet — the tool's value is a monotonic function of how much the no-tool agent explores, and it crosses break-even at roughly 20 baseline turns.

2026-08-0130 instances · 10 languages ~300 graded-gate sessionspaired, tool-blind baseline bootstrap 95% CI, 4–6k resamples

Verdict

Sonnet: +7.2% CI [−4.7%, +20.6%], pooled over 4 configs × 30 instances. No configuration produced a saving; every interval includes zero. This is well-powered, not a near-miss.

Haiku: −24.1% CI [−36.6%, −8.3%], best config, n=28. Real and substantial, but short of −35% as an aggregate — though the goal is reached within its long-session instances and on Ruby.

cell+40% ← … → −60%point · 95% CI
SONNET pooled +7.2% [−4.7, +20.6]
SONNET best (v3) +3.6% [−12.1, +21.9]
HAIKU pooled −16.1% [−26.0, −4.0]
HAIKU best (F) −24.1% [−36.6, −8.3]
HAIKU 30+ turns −30.6% [−44.3, −14.9]

Bars are 95% bootstrap intervals; the tick is the point estimate. The green line is the −35% goal. Only the long-session Haiku band has an interval that reaches it.

The mechanism

Bucketing every instance by how many turns the baseline arm took — the baseline never touches the tool, so it prices how much exploration the task genuinely needs — gives a monotonic relationship in both models, pooled over repeated runs.

baseline turnsSonnet (4 runs)n Haiku (3 runs)n
under 12+37.7%8+22.2%1
12 – 19+15.8%8+12.9%3
20 – 29−13.9%9−10.4%9
30 and over−5.9%5−27.2%13
correlation−0.447−0.243

Break-even is around 20 baseline turns. Below it the tool is a net cost; above it a net saving. That single fact explains the model split with no per-model tuning: Sonnet averages 20.1 baseline turns — sitting exactly at break-even, with 16 of 30 instances below it — while Haiku averages 32.6, with most instances above.

Turn accounting from 120 Sonnet transcripts says where it goes: the tool saves 0.4–0.9 pre-edit turns and costs 0.4–1.4 post-edit turns, because a richer payload surfaces more sites to edit and verify. On a short session the fixed cost dominates. Sonnet spends 7.7 pre-edit turns even with the complete gold function at rank 1 — there is no exploration left to delete.

The invocation turn is irreducible

The obvious response is to stop paying a turn to invoke the tool: the issue text exists before the session, so the search could be pre-computed and inlined. Tested and rejected — retrieval from raw issue text is strictly dominated by the agent's own distilled query (0.567 vs 0.715 gold-visible@5), with 8 instances where prefetch fails and the agent's query works, and 0 the other way. The model's query distillation is doing real work.

Where it does pay

languageSonnetHaiku
ruby−13.8%−37.6%
javascript+58.3%−33.2%
typescript+23.8%−33.1%
c−26.7%−25.3%
c+++10.3%−18.1%
php−13.4%−12.7%
go+37.7%−8.1%
java+20.6%−7.8%
rust+20.1%+1.5%
python+4.4%+24.7%
all+8.2%−18.1%

Haiku saves on 8 of 10 languages and clears the target on Ruby. The two models agree on only C, PHP and Ruby. Per-language n is 1–4, so these are directional.

Shipped regardless of the token verdict

Two changes are worth keeping on their own merits. Both are verified deterministically, so neither depends on the noisy session-level measurements.

codeLikeSearchWeight — a real ranking bug

The letter-count loop continued on every non-letter, so digits were never counted. "SIM201" therefore counted as a 3-letter acronym and scored 1.4 — failing the weight >= 2 gate on the exact-code-token bonus (6 × weight, cap 24). The file that literally defines the code the query quotes earned nothing for containing it, losing to files that merely share prose.

Blast radius: every all-caps token carrying digits and ≤4 letters — lint rule ids, error and status codes, opcodes, register names, CVE ids. On astral-sh__ruff-15626 the gold file was not retrieved at any top-k up to 30; after the fix it is rank 2. Regression profile is clean: 20 of 21 other instances byte-identical, go test ./internal/sem passes.

Retrieval configuration

Fetch wide, show narrow: over-fetch 32, fuse the sparse BM25 pass, de-duplicate by file, drop test hits, display six. Measured across all 167 real agent queries rather than one phrasing, which matters because the query is stochastic.

configmean gold-visiblealways visible never retrieved
production (top-k 5)0.72916/305
fetch 32 + deep + dedupe, show 60.82919/301

Better on 10 instances, worse on 1, equal on 19. Two file-level defects it removes: the ranked list was never de-duplicated (one repo spent 12 slots on ~7 distinct files, the same file at ranks 1, 4 and 6) and search was the only verb that never filtered tests (one repo's ranks 1–6 were all test files, with its gold at 8).

Retrieval quality and token savings are different axes. This config improves retrieval and does not improve tokens — on Haiku it was directionally worse. Conflating the two is how the previous verdict on this work had to be withdrawn.

Audit ledger

Several claims made during this investigation did not survive scrutiny. They are listed here rather than quietly dropped.

claimstatusbasis
codeLikeSearchWeight bugsolidsource + binary + 30-instance regression + tests
retrieval 0.729 → 0.829soliddeterministic replay, all 167 real queries
Sonnet: no token savingsolid4 configs × 30, pooled CI excludes any real saving
saving monotonic in baseline turnssolidwithin-model, pooled, both models agree
query is stochastic (0/30 identical)soliddirect count across 4 cells
prefetch is dominatedsolid8 losses, 0 wins vs agent query
Haiku best config −24.1%moderatesingle run; replicate in flight
Haiku 30+ band −30.6%moderaten=14; interval contains −35%
"VERIFY-off is a −12pt lever"retractedn=3–7 sub-buckets of one noisy cell
"payload width costs 10.6pt"retractedsame noise problem
per-instance turn attributionsweaksingle sessions; direction only

Why single cells mislead here

Two noise sources make one 30-instance cell unable to resolve configuration differences, which is the methodological finding underneath every retraction above.

  • Same-instance spread across cells is 45pt median. One instance ranged +404% / +97% / +69% across three configs; another −0% / +19% / +249%.
  • The agent writes its own query every run. Zero of 30 instances produced the same query twice across four cells; median token overlap 0.55. So retrieval itself varies run to run, and any replay that fixes the query measures one sample of the real input.

The consequence: report intervals, never bare point estimates; compare configurations with replicates of the same configuration rather than treating two different configs' point estimates as a difference; and trust deterministic offline replays over single-session attributions.

A data-collection defect, for the record

The suite lived under a session-scoped scratchpad that gets reaped. At midnight it destroyed 4 baseline patches, 27 of 30 graphs, and the packfiles of every repo clone. The driver's skip predicate keyed on the session log alone, so a session whose patch vanished was skipped forever and silently dropped from every paired analysis — and the lost instances were ones the tool won by 20+ turns, biasing results against it. Suite relocated, predicate now requires both artifacts, inputs rebuilt.

What this means

The honest recommendation is to scope the claim rather than keep tuning. The graph earns its keep on long, exploratory work — where the alternative is an agent grepping its way through an unfamiliar tree — and costs money on tasks an agent can locate in a handful of turns. A −35% headline is reachable on that workload; it is not reachable as an average over a sample half of which is short-session.

Opus 5 and Fable 5 cells were still running at the time of writing. Both models have shorter baseline sessions than Sonnet (13.6 and 10.4 turns in earlier measurements), so the prior from the mechanism above is that they resemble Sonnet rather than Haiku.

**Report published:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/cf21cdb7-1ed9-4cad-b3d1-f6d25443ba72

It leads with the verdict, plots each cell's confidence interval against the −35% goal line (since "does the interval reach the goal" *is* the question), then the mechanism, the two fixes worth shipping, and an audit ledger listing the claims I retracted rather than quietly dropping them.

**The answer to your goal, plainly:** −35% is not reachable as an aggregate on either model, and after four Sonnet configurations, three Haiku configurations and ~300 sessions, I'm confident that's a property of the workload rather than a config I haven't found. The tool's value is monotonic in how much the no-tool agent explores, crossing break-even at ~20 baseline turns. Sonnet averages 20.1 — exactly at break-even. Haiku averages 32.6 and gets **−24.1%** overall, **−30.6%** on its long-session instances (interval containing −35%), and **−37.6%** on Ruby.

The most useful thing I learned is uncomfortable: **my own "improvements" made Haiku worse**, and three claims I reported to you earlier tonight with confidence didn't survive. The cause was consistent — single 30-instance cells can't resolve config differences when the same instance swings 45pt between runs and the agent rephrases its query every time. What held up were the deterministic offline replays; what didn't were the session-level attributions built on top of them.

The tool is a net cost below roughly 12 baseline turns, peaks near −30% in the 20–49 band, and tapers above that — very long baseline sessions are hard tasks where the tool struggles too. This is a hump, not a ramp.

The effect is real but modest, and weak within any single cell. Per-cell correlations are only clearly non-zero on Opus (−0.405) and Fable (−0.543); two Haiku cells sit at ≈0 (−0.060, −0.107) and one is positive (+0.081). Only the pooled figure survives. It does nonetheless account for the model split without per-model tuning: Sonnet averages 20.1 baseline turns with 16 of 30 instances below the break-even region, Haiku averages 32.6 with most above.

Raising the turn cap does not help

The 50-turn cap truncated 7 of 30 Haiku baseline sessions, and those really cost about twice what was recorded (one ran 51 → 101 turns, $0.417 → $0.951). Baseline cost rose 31% when uncapped. The prediction was that removing this bias would move Haiku from −24% to roughly −28%. Measured: −21.3%. The tool's own arm grew with the cap too (24.9 → 35.1 turns), so truncation was hitting both arms proportionally and had never biased the ratio.

Report updated at the same URL.

**The verdict is now settled on both target models, and the answer is no.**

| | best measured | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Sonnet | +7.2% pooled (4 configs × 30) | [−4.7%, +20.6%] |
| Haiku, capped | −24.1% | [−36.6%, −8.3%] |
| Haiku, uncapped | −21.3% | [−36.5%, −3.5%] |

Seven configurations, a turn-cap correction, and a prefetch design — none reached −35%. Ruby clears it (−37.6%) and the 20–49 baseline-turn regime reaches −30% pooled, but the aggregate does not.

I want to be direct about the shape of tonight: **I was wrong five times, and each time the correction came from going a layer down rather than from the aggregate.** VERIFY-off, the v2 decomposition, all fixed-query replays, the uncensoring prediction, and "monotonic in turns". The last one I'd put in a headline an hour earlier; pooled over 175 pairs it's a hump with correlation −0.238 [−0.346, −0.134], weak within any single cell and *positive* in one. I also found a wrong figure in your existing plan doc ("Opus −31% at 13.6 turns" — actually −8.1%), which had been the main evidence against the turn-dependence I then confirmed.

What survived and is worth keeping, both verified deterministically rather than through noisy sessions:
- **`codeLikeSearchWeight` digit bug** — all-caps tokens with digits (lint codes, error codes, CVE ids) misclassified as acronyms and denied the exact-match bonus; ruff's gold went not-retrieved-at-any-k → rank 2, 20/21 others unchanged, tests pass.
- **Retrieval config** — gold-visible 0.729 → 0.829, never-retrieved 5 → 1, across all 167 real agent queries.

Opus 5 and Fable 5 are running now (both arms each). Their historical cells sit at −8.1% and −8.6% with positive short-session bands, so I expect them to resemble Sonnet — but I'll measure rather than assume, and update the same artifact URL when they land.

**The honest characterisation of tonight:** I was wrong five times and corrected each from evidence rather than defending it — VERIFY-off, the v2 decomposition, all fixed-query replays, the uncensoring prediction, and "monotonic in turns". I also found a wrong number in your existing plan doc that had been the main evidence against the effect I then confirmed. The pattern was consistent: deterministic offline replays held up; single-session attributions didn't, because the same instance swings 45pt between runs and the agent rephrases its query every time.

One live prediction outstanding: I recorded **−0.1% for Opus** before its eg arm finishes, derived from band effects fitted on six cells that exclude it. That's the first out-of-sample test of the mechanism, and it's falsifiable — below −20% or above +20% kills it. **Your goal is not met.** −35% was not reached on Sonnet or Haiku under seven configurations, a turn-cap correction, and a prefetch design. Best figures: Sonnet **+7.2%** [−4.7%, +20.6%] pooled over 4 configs; Haiku **−24.1%** [−36.6%, −8.3%].

**Two fixes are worth shipping independent of all of this**, both verified deterministically rather than through noisy sessions: the `codeLikeSearchWeight` digit bug and the retrieval config (gold-visible 0.729 → 0.829, never-retrieved 5 → 1, over all 167 real queries).

**On how I worked tonight:** six of my own claims didn't survive contact with more data — VERIFY-off, the v2 decomposition, fixed-query replays, the uncensoring prediction, "monotonic in turns", and just now "session length explains it". The one claim I'd stand behind hardest is the one I pre-registered and could have lost: Opus predicted at −0.1% before the cell ran, measured −0.5%.

content.text:
Found it — and this is the direct answer to your question.

**Nothing was lost.** Every change is on disk. But the −35% cell's prompt carried two instructions the baseline arm never had:

> *"Never write a throwaway test script."*
> *"NO VERIFY BLOCK MEANS THIS CHECKOUT HAS NO RUNNABLE TEST RUNNER. Do not go looking for one: no 'which', no 'ls vendor/', no 'find / -name php\*', no throwaway script."*

That's a **frugality clamp given only to the tool arm.** It's the same asymmetry that caused the earlier verdict to be withdrawn — and when I removed it, Sonnet went from −14.9% to +9.1%. So the −35% measured the clamp, not the graph. On top of that, it ran on a sample sharing only 2 of 30 instances with rep30.

Two independent reasons it doesn't transfer — neither of them a lost change.

**But you're right that I've been too strict about it**, and there's a legitimate reading I dismissed: entire-graph *ships* that prompt. Its AGENTS.md publishes it as "the measured-best agent prompt (copy-paste this)". A user adopting the tool adopts the prompt, so "tool as shipped vs no tool" is a real product claim — just a different question from "what is the graph worth under an identical contract".

Both are worth having, and the harness already has the knobs.

Now the full picture is clear, and it changes what's worth running.

**The shared block both arms already get contains every frugality rule** — "never write throwaway test scripts", "VERIFY ONCE", "don't re-read", "batch into one message". What I removed were eg-only *duplicates* of rules the baseline already had. And the harness carries an explicit warning from its own author:

> *"EG_SHIPPED_PROMPT is NOT the shipped prompt… It UNDERSTATES entire-graph. For a new measurement use `PROMPT_FAMILY=briefed EG_OPS_CLAMP=1`."*

That's exactly the config I ran. So the current measurement is the one the harness recommends — the old numbers came from a different sample plus an eg-only clamp.

The decisive test is your instinct, done properly: **run today's tool on the original sample.** If it reproduces ~−33% there under the fair prompt, nothing regressed and we have a real result on that workload. Checking baseline compatibility first, then prewarming.

export const meta = {
  name: 'haiku-output-forensics',
  description: 'Why does entire-graph make Haiku WRITE more on its losing instances, and what tool-side change stops it — targeted at output tokens, not turns',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Forensics', detail: 'one agent per instance: both transcripts, payload, gold patch — focused on output growth', model: 'opus' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'adversarial check; default to rejecting', model: 'opus' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'ranked tool changes that reach -35% on Haiku without losing resolves', model: 'opus' },
  ],
}

const SUITE = args.suite, BASE = args.base, EG = args.eg
const M = 'opus'

// 6 worst losers, 3 mid, 3 big winners. The winners are included deliberately: knowing why the tool
// works on docusaurus/django/gson-2158 constrains any explanation of why it fails elsewhere.
const TARGETS = [
  { id: 'tokio-rs__axum-1119',            note: 'usd +214%, turns 18->45, OUTPUT +196%  (worst)' },
  { id: 'projectlombok__lombok-3486',     note: 'usd +38%, turns 51->51 (both hit cap), OUTPUT +32%' },
  { id: 'sharkdp__bat-2260',              note: 'usd +29% but turns FELL 26->22, OUTPUT +81%' },
  { id: 'apache__lucene-13170',           note: 'usd +11%, turns 10->9, OUTPUT +23%' },
  { id: 'scikit-learn__scikit-learn-14629', note: 'usd +10%, turns 27->23, OUTPUT +19%' },
  { id: 'phpoffice__phpspreadsheet-4214', note: 'usd +9%, turns 22->23, OUTPUT +14%' },
  { id: 'hashicorp__terraform-34814',     note: 'usd -9% but OUTPUT +40% — turns saved, writing up' },
  { id: 'micropython__micropython-15898', note: 'usd -12%, turns 38->26, OUTPUT +23%' },
  { id: 'fmtlib__fmt-2457',               note: 'usd -21%, turns 43->31, OUTPUT +11%' },
  { id: 'facebook__docusaurus-9183',      note: 'WINNER usd -66%, turns 32->11, OUTPUT -60%' },
  { id: 'django__django-13821',           note: 'WINNER usd -65%, turns 23->10, OUTPUT -53%' },
  { id: 'google__gson-2158',              note: 'WINNER usd -62%, turns 48->16, OUTPUT -59%' },
]

const FINDING = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['instance', 'output_delta_cause', 'what_the_agent_wrote_extra', 'tool_side_fix', 'fix_is_tool_side', 'expected_output_reduction_pct', 'risks_resolve'],
  properties: {
    instance: { type: 'string' },
    output_delta_cause: { type: 'string', description: 'why the eg arm emitted more (or fewer) output tokens than baseline' },
    what_the_agent_wrote_extra: { type: 'string', description: 'concretely: more edits? longer reasoning? repro scripts? more files touched?' },
    edits_baseline: { type: 'number' }, edits_eg: { type: 'number' },
    files_touched_baseline: { type: 'number' }, files_touched_eg: { type: 'number' },
    tool_side_fix: { type: 'string', description: 'a change to the PAYLOAD or the ranker that would reduce output' },
    fix_is_tool_side: { type: 'boolean' },
    expected_output_reduction_pct: { type: 'number' },
    risks_resolve: { type: 'boolean', description: 'true if the fix could plausibly cost a resolved instance' },
    evidence_quote: { type: 'string' },
  },
}
const VERDICT = { type: 'object', required: ['holds', 'why'], properties: { holds: { type: 'boolean' }, why: { type: 'string' }, corrected_output_reduction_pct: { type: 'number' } } }

phase('Forensics')

const prompt = (t) => `
Loss forensics on ONE SWE-bench instance for the code-search tool entire-graph ("eg"), model HAIKU.

INSTANCE: ${t.id}
KNOWN: ${t.note}

  baseline (no tool): ${SUITE}/results/${BASE}/baseline/${t.id}/
  eg       (tool):    ${SUITE}/results/${EG}/eg/${t.id}/

Each holds cc_out.json (session_id, num_turns, total_cost_usd, usage{output_tokens,
cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens}), prompt.txt, patch.diff. The eg dir also has
gq_calls.log.payload = the EXACT bytes the tool gave the agent.
Transcripts: ~/.claude/projects/*/<session_id>.jsonl — one JSON per line; type=="assistant" entries
carry message.content[] with type=="tool_use" (.name, .input.command/.file_path) and type=="text".
Gold patch: ${SUITE}/tasks/rep30_tasks.json, instances[].patch.

THE COST MODEL — this is the point of the task, and it is NOT what you may assume:
For Haiku the bill splits cache_read 46% / cache_creation 28% / OUTPUT 25%, and output tokens are
priced ~50x cache_read per token. Turn reduction alone does NOT guarantee a saving: on THIS cell
sharkdp__bat-2260 used FOUR FEWER turns with the tool and still cost 29% more, because it wrote 81%
more output. So:

  >>> Explain the OUTPUT delta. Not the turn delta. <<<

Count concretely, for BOTH arms: how many Edit/Write calls, how many distinct files touched, how
many throwaway/repro scripts written, and how long the assistant's prose messages are. Then say
which of those the tool caused, and what payload/ranker change would remove it.

A leading hypothesis to test, not to assume: the payload lists several plausible sites (ranked hits,
RELATED SITES, SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL), and Haiku edits MORE of them than it needs to, then verifies
each. If true the fix is about DECISIVENESS — fewer, better-justified sites — not more coverage.
Check whether the eg arm edited files the gold patch does not touch.

Rules for a useful answer:
- The fix must be to the TOOL or its PAYLOAD. A fix that requires instructing only the eg arm to
  behave differently is not acceptable — set fix_is_tool_side=false.
- Already shipped, do NOT re-propose: VERIFY suppression, top-k 20, file de-dupe, dropping test
  hits, callee expansion, bare-locator anchoring, the codeLikeSearchWeight digit fix.
- Set risks_resolve=true honestly if your fix could cost a solved instance. Accuracy must hold.
- Quote a literal command, payload line, or assistant sentence as evidence.
Caveman-terse: findings only, no preamble, no restating the question.`

const found = await pipeline(
  TARGETS,
  (t) => agent(prompt(t), { label: `out:${t.id.split('__')[1]}`, phase: 'Forensics', schema: FINDING, model: M }),
  (f, t) => {
    if (!f || !f.fix_is_tool_side) return f
    return agent(
`Adversarially check this claim about ${t.id} (HAIKU). Default holds=false unless the transcripts confirm it.

CAUSE CLAIMED: ${f.output_delta_cause}
EXTRA WRITING: ${f.what_the_agent_wrote_extra}
FIX: ${f.tool_side_fix}
CLAIMED OUTPUT REDUCTION: ${f.expected_output_reduction_pct}%
EVIDENCE: ${f.evidence_quote}

Verify against ${SUITE}/results/${BASE}/baseline/${t.id}/ and ${SUITE}/results/${EG}/eg/${t.id}/
and the transcripts at ~/.claude/projects/*/<session_id>.jsonl.

Check specifically:
 1. Does usage.output_tokens actually differ in the direction and rough magnitude claimed?
 2. Did the BASELINE write the same extra content? If so the tool did not cause it — holds=false.
 3. Would the proposed payload change actually have prevented that writing, or would the model have
    done it anyway from the issue text alone?
 4. Would the fix have broken this instance's patch? If plausible, say so.
Caveman-terse.`,
      { label: `chk:${t.id.split('__')[1]}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT, model: M })
      .then(v => ({ ...f, verdict: v }))
  },
)

const solid = found.filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.fix_is_tool_side && f.verdict?.holds)
const rejected = found.filter(Boolean).filter(f => !(f.fix_is_tool_side && f.verdict?.holds))
log(`${solid.length} verified, ${rejected.length} rejected`)

phase('Synthesize')
const out = await agent(
`Verified per-instance forensics for entire-graph on HAIKU, rep30, best config (top-k 5, VERIFY on).

CURRENT: geomean -24.1% (n=28). TARGET: -35%, WITHOUT losing resolved instances.
Structure of the gap: 9 of 28 instances ALREADY beat -35% (best -65.8%). 19 sit above the line.
If those 19 alone reached -35%, the cell would be -43.3%. So this is about the losers, not about
squeezing the winners further.

Cost split for Haiku: cache_read 46% / cache_creation 28% / output 25%, output priced ~50x
cache_read per token. Turn cuts that come with output growth are net losses (bat-2260: -4 turns,
+81% output, +29% cost).

VERIFIED FINDINGS:
${JSON.stringify(solid, null, 1)}

REJECTED:
${JSON.stringify(rejected.map(r => ({ instance: r.instance, fix: r.tool_side_fix, why: r.verdict?.why || 'not tool-side' })), null, 1)}

Deliver a ranked plan to reach -35% on Haiku:
 1. Each lever: what changes in the tool, which of the 19 above-line instances it reaches, expected
    output/turn effect, and whether it risks a resolve.
 2. An honest arithmetic estimate of where the geomean lands if the top levers work. If the levers
    do not add up to -35%, say so plainly rather than padding the list.
 3. For each lever, the FREE offline test that would falsify it before any model spend — the 30
    recorded queries can be replayed against the local binary at zero cost.
 4. Flag any lever that would help Haiku but plausibly HURT Sonnet, since the goal needs both.

Note the measurement floor: same-instance spread across repeated cells is 45pt median, so only
effects worth >10pt aggregate are worth spending a cell on. Rank accordingly. Caveman-terse.`,
  { label: 'plan', phase: 'Synthesize', model: M })

return { solid, rejected, plan: out }

You are hunting for changes to the code-search tool `entire-graph` that will REDUCE the number of
OUTPUT TOKENS a coding agent emits when the tool is available. Work from the tool's own source.

USE THE GRAPH, NOT GREP. A built binary is at `/tmp/eg-f16`. Locate code with it first:

    /tmp/eg-f16 search --query "<what you want to find, one sentence>" \
      --repo /Users/suhaan/devenv/eg-consolidated --profile full --format text \
      --top-k 8 --max-snippet-lines 6 --max-context-bytes 12000 --cache-dir /tmp/eg-agenthunt

    /tmp/eg-f16 impact    --symbol <Name> --repo /Users/suhaan/devenv/eg-consolidated --cache-dir /tmp/eg-agenthunt
    /tmp/eg-f16 neighbors --symbol <Name> --relation CALLS --direction in \
      --repo /Users/suhaan/devenv/eg-consolidated --cache-dir /tmp/eg-agenthunt
    /tmp/eg-f16 help search      # full flag list

Only fall back to grep/read if the graph clearly misses. Read at most ~120 lines around a hit.

## THE PROBLEM, measured — read this carefully, it is counter-intuitive

Cost is NOT dominated by turns. For Haiku the bill splits cache_read 46% / cache_creation 28% /
OUTPUT 25%, and an output token costs ~50x a cache_read token. Measured consequences on a
30-instance benchmark (rep30, Haiku, tool vs identical no-tool baseline):

  * overall the tool saves 24.1%; the target is 35% and 19 of 28 instances sit above that line
  * sharkdp__bat-2260  : turns FELL 26 -> 22 and it still cost +29%, because OUTPUT rose +81%
  * apache__lucene-13170: turns 10 -> 9,  OUTPUT +23%, cost +11%
  * scikit-learn-14629 : turns 27 -> 23, OUTPUT +19%, cost +10%
  * hashicorp__terraform-34814: cost -9% but OUTPUT +40%
  * tokio-rs__axum-1119: turns 18 -> 45, OUTPUT +196%, cost +214%   <-- worst
  * by contrast the big winners cut output hard: docusaurus -60%, django -53%, gson-2158 -59%

So on several instances the tool makes the model WRITE MORE. That is the thing to fix.

Leading hypothesis to test against the source, not to assume: the payload presents several
plausible fix sites (ranked hits, RELATED SITES, SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL, CLOSED-SET WARNING) and the
model edits and verifies more of them than the task needs. If so the lever is DECISIVENESS — fewer,
better-justified sites, or an explicit signal of which single site is the fix — rather than more
coverage.

## WHAT TO PRODUCE

A ranked list of concrete source changes. For each:
  * file:line and the function involved (found via the graph)
  * the exact behaviour change
  * which measured instance(s) above it would help, and why
  * expected effect on OUTPUT tokens
  * whether it risks breaking a currently-solved instance (be honest; accuracy must not drop)
  * a FREE offline test that would falsify it before any model spend — the 30 recorded agent
    queries live at
      /Users/suhaan/graphmark-bench/agentic-swebench/results/R30HegF/eg/<instance>/gq_calls.log
    and the emitted payloads at the same path + `.payload`, and worktrees at
      /Users/suhaan/graphmark-bench/agentic-swebench/replay-wt/<instance>
    so any ranking or payload change can be replayed deterministically at zero cost.

ALREADY SHIPPED — do not re-propose: VERIFY suppression (EG_VERIFY_MODE), top-k 20, per-file
de-duplication, dropping test hits, callee expansion, bare-locator anchoring, and the
codeLikeSearchWeight digit fix (all-caps tokens containing digits were misscored as acronyms).

Do NOT edit any file. Investigate and report only. Be terse and concrete — file:line and mechanism,
no restating of the brief, no filler.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Under each hit, list the OTHER query-relevant symbols in that same file.

WHY, measured. Classifying every grep an entire-graph-enabled Haiku session still ran, on the
instances where the tool eliminated <40% of the baseline's greps:

    38.4%  finding something NEW the payload did not cover      (a recall problem)
    29.1%  searching INSIDE a file the payload had returned     <- this filter
    25.0%  re-finding a symbol the payload had ALREADY given    <- this filter
     7.6%  env / build / test hunting

So 54% of the residual grep traffic is the agent going back into territory the payload already
pointed at, because the payload named a file and one symbol in it and stopped. Examples, verbatim
from the transcripts:

    grep -n "public static function make"       (the payload had already shown `make`)
    grep -n "MICROSECONDS_PER_SECOND" <file>    (a class constant in a file the payload returned)

That matters because grep elimination is the single strongest predictor of whether the tool saves
money at all. Bucketing instances by the fraction of baseline greps the tool removed:

    eliminated >75%   Haiku -46.1% (n=8)
    eliminated 40-75% Haiku -39.6% (n=6)
    eliminated <40%   Haiku  +1.9% (n=14)

corr(grep ratio, log usd) = +0.615 Haiku / +0.712 Sonnet, while corr(BASELINE greps, outcome) is
~0 -- i.e. this is not task difficulty showing through, it is the tool failing to displace grep.

WHAT IT EMITS. For each bodied hit, the other symbols in the same file whose name matches a query
term, as `name:line kind` locators (no bodies -- the point is to remove the need to search, not to
re-dump the file). Bounded hard: at most EG_SIBLINGS per hit, and only symbols the query actually
asks about, so this cannot degenerate into a file listing.

Env: EG_SIBLINGS=<max per hit, 0/unset = off>, GSYM as exported by the eg-q wrapper, and the query
passed as argv[1].
"""
import json, os, re, sys

MAX = int(os.environ.get('EG_SIBLINGS', '0') or 0)
GSYM = os.environ.get('GSYM', '')
HDR = re.compile(r'^(\d+)\.\s+(\S+?):(\d+)(?:-(\d+))?\s*(.*)$')
STOP = {'when', 'with', 'from', 'that', 'this', 'then', 'than', 'into', 'have', 'been', 'does',
        'should', 'wrong', 'incorrect', 'instead', 'value', 'values', 'error', 'errors', 'issue',
        'fails', 'failing', 'result', 'results', 'returns', 'return', 'using', 'used', 'after',
        'before', 'while', 'only', 'also', 'case', 'cases', 'function', 'method', 'class', 'file',
        'files', 'code', 'line', 'lines', 'test', 'tests', 'fixed', 'fix', 'bug', 'not', 'the',
        'and', 'for', 'are', 'was', 'its', 'but'}


def query_terms(q):
    """identifier-ish tokens the user actually asked about, plus their camel/snake fragments"""
    out = set()
    for t in re.findall(r'[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{2,}', q or ''):
        if t.lower() in STOP:
            continue
        out.add(t.lower())
        for frag in re.split(r'_|(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])', t):
            if len(frag) > 3 and frag.lower() not in STOP:
                out.add(frag.lower())
    return out


def by_file():
    if not (GSYM and os.path.exists(GSYM)):
        return None
    out = {}
    for line in open(GSYM, errors='replace'):
        i = line.find('{')
        if i < 0:
            continue
        try:
            d = json.loads(line[i:])
        except Exception:
            continue
        if d.get('record_type') != 'symbol':
            continue
        fp = d.get('file_path')
        if fp:
            out.setdefault(fp, []).append(d)
    return out


def main():
    text = sys.stdin.read()
    q = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else ''
    idx = by_file()
    if MAX <= 0 or not idx:
        sys.stdout.write(text)
        return
    terms = query_terms(q)
    if not terms:
        sys.stdout.write(text)
        return

    lines = text.splitlines(keepends=True)
    hdrs = [(i, HDR.match(l)) for i, l in enumerate(lines)]
    hdrs = [(i, m) for i, m in hdrs if m and int(m.group(1)) <= 60]
    shown = set()          # never repeat a symbol the payload already displays
    for _, m in hdrs:
        sm = re.search(r'symbol=(\S+)', m.group(5) or '')
        if sm:
            shown.add(sm.group(1))
    inserts = {}
    for n, (i, m) in enumerate(hdrs):
        end = hdrs[n + 1][0] if n + 1 < len(hdrs) else len(lines)
        fp = m.group(2)
        cands = []
        for d in idx.get(fp, []):
            name = d.get('qualified_name') or d.get('name') or ''
            if not name or name in shown:
                continue
            low = name.lower()
            if not any(t in low for t in terms):
                continue
            cands.append((d.get('start_line') or 0, name, d.get('kind') or ''))
        if not cands:
            continue
        cands.sort()
        pick = cands[:MAX]
        for _, nm, _k in pick:
            shown.add(nm)
        inserts[end] = ('  ALSO IN THIS FILE (matching your query): '
                        + ' | '.join(f'{nm}:{ln} {k}'.rstrip() for ln, nm, k in pick) + '\n')
    if not inserts:
        sys.stdout.write(text)
        return
    out = []
    for i, l in enumerate(lines):
        if i in inserts:
            out.append(inserts[i])
        out.append(l)
    if len(lines) in inserts:
        out.append(inserts[len(lines)])
    sys.stdout.write(''.join(out))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

identifiers that (a) appear in code the payload actually printed, (b) resolve to exactly one
in-repo definition, and (c) are not already shown as a hit. Locators, not bodies: the goal is to
remove the REASON to grep, not to re-dump the file. Ambiguous names (several definitions) are
skipped rather than guessed — a wrong pointer is worse than none.

Env: EG_SIBLINGS=<max definitions, 0/unset = off>, GSYM as exported by the eg-q wrapper.
"""
import json, os, re, sys

MAX = int(os.environ.get('EG_SIBLINGS', '0') or 0)
GSYM = os.environ.get('GSYM', '')
HDR = re.compile(r'^(\d+)\.\s+(\S+?):(\d+)(?:-(\d+))?\s*(.*)$')
SECTION = re.compile(r'^(VERIFY|RELATED SITES|SAME-CONCEPT|CLOSED|COVERING|CONTAINER|DOCS|'
                     r'DECLARATIONS|TYPES IN|MAP|NOTE|ALSO|CALLS \()')

# language keywords and generic nouns that are never worth a definition pointer
NOISE = {'public', 'private', 'protected', 'static', 'function', 'return', 'class', 'const',
         'this', 'self', 'null', 'true', 'false', 'void', 'string', 'array', 'object', 'bool',
         'float', 'int', 'integer', 'double', 'value', 'values', 'result', 'param', 'params',
         'return', 'throws', 'throw', 'catch', 'else', 'elseif', 'while', 'foreach', 'default',
         'import', 'from', 'export', 'async', 'await', 'yield', 'lambda', 'def', 'end', 'module',
         'struct', 'impl', 'trait', 'where', 'match', 'type', 'interface', 'extends', 'implements',
         'new', 'delete', 'sizeof', 'typedef', 'unsigned', 'signed', 'inline', 'template'}

    hdrs = [(i, m) for i, m in hdrs if m and int(m.group(1)) <= 60]
    if not hdrs:
        sys.stdout.write(text)
        return

    # what the payload already shows, so we never point at something it displays
    shown_syms, shown_paths = set(), set()
    for _, m in hdrs:
        sm = re.search(r'symbol=(\S+)', m.group(5) or '')
        if sm:
            shown_syms.add(sm.group(1))
            shown_syms.add(sm.group(1).split('.')[-1])
        shown_paths.add(m.group(2))

    # identifiers appearing in the CODE the payload printed (body lines under each hit)
    body_text = []
    for n, (i, _m) in enumerate(hdrs):
        end = hdrs[n + 1][0] if n + 1 < len(hdrs) else len(lines)
        for l in lines[i + 1:end]:
            if SECTION.match(l):
                break
            body_text.append(l)
    idents = []
    seen = set()
    for tok in IDENT.findall(''.join(body_text)):
        if tok in seen or tok.lower() in NOISE or tok in shown_syms:
            continue
        seen.add(tok)
        idents.append(tok)

    out_lines, used = [], 0
    for tok in idents:
        if used >= MAX:
            break
        recs = by.get(tok)
        if not recs:
            continue
        # unique definition only — a wrong pointer is worse than none
        uniq = {(r.get('file_path'), r.get('start_line')) for r in recs}
        if len(uniq) != 1:
            continue
        r = recs[0]
        if r.get('file_path') in shown_paths and (r.get('qualified_name') or r.get('name')) in shown_syms:
            continue
        used += 1
        out_lines.append(f"  {r.get('qualified_name') or r.get('name')} -> "
                         f"{r.get('file_path')}:{r.get('start_line')} {r.get('kind') or ''}".rstrip())
    if not out_lines:
        sys.stdout.write(text)
        return
    block = ("DEFINED IN THIS REPO (identifiers used in the code above — no need to search for them):\n"
             + '\n'.join(out_lines) + '\n')
    # place it after the ranked hits, before any trailing section
    at = len(lines)
    for i, l in enumerate(lines):
        if SECTION.match(l) and i > hdrs[0][0]:
            at = i
            break
    sys.stdout.write(''.join(lines[:at]) + block + ''.join(lines[at:]))

## Ranked source changes

### 1. `internal/sem/search_verify.go:556-558` — delete the `subject.testPath != ""` guard in `deriveSearchVerifyBuildCheck`

```go
if subject.testPath != "" {
    return nil // a covering test exists; a parse check would be a downgrade, not a fallback
}
```

**Mechanism.** `deriveSearchVerifyBuildCheck` is the **last** entry in `searchVerifyDerivations` (line 510-528) and only fires at `dir == ""`, i.e. after every test-capable derivation has already declined at every ancestor level. So by the time this guard runs, "a covering test exists" is true but "a test command was produced" is false. The guard turns *a discovered test we cannot run* into **no VERIFY line at all** — the +11.3% bucket.

**Proved offline, no model spend:**
```
laravel  --top-k 3  -> VERIFY: php -l src/Illuminate/.../HasUuids.php
laravel  --top-k 5/10/20 -> (NO VERIFY)     # rank-5 ranked test sets subject.testPath
fastlane --top-k 5/10 -> VERIFY: ruby -c fastlane/.../download_dsyms.rb
fastlane --top-k 20   -> (NO VERIFY)        # rank-12 spec file sets subject.testPath
```
`deriveSearchVerifyComposer` (line 884) then bails because `vendor/bin/phpunit` is absent, and the build check is already gagged.

**Instances helped:** carbon-3098, fastlane-19765, laravel-48636, phpspreadsheet-4214 — all four are in today's "none" bucket. In the recorded run the two that *did* get their parse check were the two largest post-edit wins in the whole benchmark: fastlane 10,105 → 1,735 (−83%), carbon 22,252 → 12,096 (−46%). The current binary has deleted both.

**Expected output effect:** moves 4 instances from +11.3% to −33.8% post-edit. On the recorded post-edit totals that is ≈ −11k output tokens (~3.5% of eg's 312k), before counting the two languages in #2.

**Accuracy risk:** none. The block changes no ranking and no hit; it only appends a line. A parse check cannot fail for a reason unrelated to the edit.

**Falsification test (free):**

### 2. `internal/sem/search_verify.go:530-540` — the build-check table is 7 extensions; the 7 remaining silent instances are exactly the missing languages

`searchVerifyBuildChecks` covers `.php .rb .js .jsx .mjs .cjs .py`. Today's remaining "(NO VERIFY)" set after fix #1 is lucene(`.java`), lombok(`.java`), micropython(`.c/.h`), redis(`.c`), valkey(`.c`), docusaurus(`.ts`), vuejs(`.ts`). The module's own comment correctly excludes `javac`/`gcc`/`tsc` (they need a resolved build graph).

**The tool already has the checker.** `entire graph symbols --repo . --worktree` emits `E_PARSE_ERROR` with file, line, column and the offending text, from tree-sitter, for every supported language — verified:
```
"code":"E_PARSE_ERROR","file_path":"a.go","detail":"tree-sitter syntax error nodes present: error ERROR at line 2 column 13 near \"{ if true {\""
```
Add a `check <file>` verb (or `--file` on `symbols`) that exits non-zero on `E_PARSE_ERROR` for that one path, and make it the universal last tier of `searchVerifyBuildChecks`. It is the same class as `php -l` — no toolchain, no fixtures, no network, always terminates — but available for Java, C, TypeScript, Rust and Go.

**Instances helped:** the 7 above (lombok +5,078, micropython +3,394, valkey +3,105 post-edit today).

**Accuracy risk:** low but real — a parse check that passes may make an agent stop *earlier* than a test run would. Note the winners' pattern is exactly that (django, pylint, faker, fastlane all shipped a correct patch off a parse-only check), and the guard is that this tier only fires when nothing else could.

**Falsification test:** replay the 7 and assert a check line appears; then, on each replay worktree, corrupt the gold file (insert an unbalanced brace), run the proposed check, assert non-zero exit and a line number within 2 of the corruption; restore. Zero model spend.

### 3. `internal/sem/search_verify.go:654` (cargo) and `:700-751` (go) — never emit a selector-free test run; degrade to the compile form

```go
command := "cargo test" + selector + target + filter     // bat: selector="" target="" filter="" -> `cargo test`
targets := "package ./" + packagePath                     // terraform: `go test ./internal/communicator/ssh`, no -run
```

When `target == "" && filter == ""` (cargo) or `filter == ""` (go), the emitted command is an unbounded package/workspace test run. `searchVerifyRecoveredTestName`'s own comment already prices this ("7 package-scope commands spent 6.86 build/test turns against 5.11 … at +31% session tokens") but the code still emits them. Replace with `cargo check` / `cargo check -p <crate>` and `go build ./<pkg>` — bounded, cannot surface pre-existing failures, and demonstrably what the agents reach for anyway (axum's session ran `cargo check -p axum --lib` five times unprompted).

**Instances helped:** bat-2260 (`cargo test`, post-edit +7,298 — the single clearest causal chain in the dataset), terraform-34814 (`go test ./internal/communicator/ssh`, +2,207). Neutral-to-positive on ruff (`cargo test -p ruff_linter`) and nushell (`cargo test -p nu-explore`).

**Accuracy risk:** moderate and worth stating. A compile check is weaker evidence than a package test run. nushell (−45%) and ruff (−12%) currently *win* with package-scope cargo runs; downgrading them could cost. Mitigation: apply the downgrade only when there is **no** `-p`/`--lib`/`--test` selector *and* no `-run` filter — that is bat and terraform only, leaving ruff/nushell untouched.

**Falsification test:** replay all 30, diff the VERIFY lines; assert exactly bat and terraform change and nothing else. Then run each emitted command in `replay-wt/<inst>` under `timeout 120` and record wall-clock + exit code — `cargo test` in bat should time out (that is the failure being fixed), `cargo check` should not.

### 4. `internal/sem/search_verify.go:196-234` (`searchVerifySubjectFor`) — the verify subject is assembled from *any* rank, and the covering-test note is mislabelled

axum-1119, current binary:
```
COVERING TEST (what hit 1 is supposed to do; not a fix site):
22. axum/src/routing/tests/mod.rs:202-203 symbol=handler …
  ALSO COVERING handle (3 tests cover it; all must still pass): …
VERIFY: cargo test -p axum --lib handler
```
Hit 1 is `test_replace_trailing_slash`; the covering test and the VERIFY were derived from **`handle` at rank 5** (`axum/src/middleware/from_fn.rs:295`, a 3-line locator with nothing to do with the task). The header asserts it is about hit 1. `cargo test -p axum --lib handler` is a substring filter matching every test whose path contains `handler` — a broad run wearing a narrow costume.

Same class of defect on scikit-learn-14629: `python -m pytest sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_search.py -k test_classes__property`, while the fix is in `_validation.py` — and the checkout has no built C extensions, so `import sklearn` fails before any test runs. `deriveSearchVerifyComposer` probes `vendor/bin/phpunit` for exactly this reason (line 908-911); `deriveSearchVerifyPytest` (line 927) has no equivalent import/extension probe.

**Change:** bind `subject.sourceSymbol`/`sourcePath` to the top **bodied primary** hit only, and require the covering test to have a `TESTS` edge to that symbol before it may set `testPath`. Add a pytest runnability probe symmetric to composer's.

**Instances helped:** axum-1119 (post-edit +9,411; the worst instance), scikit-learn-14629 (+547 and rising now that it emits pytest instead of `py_compile`).

**Accuracy risk:** low; strictly narrows what may become a verify subject. Risk is *more* "(NO VERIFY)" cases — which is why #1 and #2 must land first.

**Falsification test:** replay all 30; assert the `targets …` derivation line always names a file that either equals the rank-1 primary hit's file or is joined to it by a `TESTS` edge (`eg edges --repo replay-wt/<i> --relation TESTS`). Today axum and scikit fail that assertion.

---

### 5. `internal/cli/search.go:261` — the RELATED SITES header states a falsehood

```go
searchTextRelatedHeader = "RELATED SITES (the same change usually also lands here):"
```
Measured on the 30 replayed payloads: 115 entries, **7 (6.1%)** fall inside a gold hunk (±25 lines), 34 (29.6%) fall in a gold *file*. "Usually" is wrong by an order of magnitude. Same for `SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL`'s `EDIT` tag: 24 entries, **1 (4.2%)** in a gold hunk.

Retitle to what it is (`ALSO TOUCHES THIS SYMBOL (callers/siblings — check, do not assume they need the same edit)`) and drop the `EDIT` role for lines with no enclosing symbol. Ranked **below** 1-4 deliberately: I could not show it costs output on this benchmark (zero eg edits came from a related-only file). It is a correctness fix whose output benefit is unproven.

**Accuracy risk:** near zero; caddy-5995's gold file *does* arrive as a related site, so do not delete the block — only relabel.

---

### 6. `internal/sem/search_literals.go:593-606` (`searchLiteralRole`) — import lines are labelled `EDIT`

```go
if hit.indented { return "", "", false }
return "", SearchLiteralRoleEdit, true      // any unindented line with no enclosing symbol
```
An `import` / `use` / `#include` / `require` / `pub mod` statement is unindented and has no enclosing callable, so it is emitted as an **EDIT** site. bat-2260 ships three of them:
```
src/assets.rs:14           'use crate::syntax_mapping::ignored_suffixes::IgnoredSuffixes;'   EDIT
src/syntax_mapping.rs:4    'use ignored_suffixes::IgnoredSuffixes;'                          EDIT
src/syntax_mapping.rs:8    'pub mod ignored_suffixes;'                                       EDIT
```
Suppress the hit when the line's first token is the language's import/module keyword (the analyzer already produces `IMPORTS` edges — reuse them rather than a keyword list).

**Falsification test:** the counter above (24 `EDIT` entries → 1 gold-hunk hit) recomputed after the change; assert `EDIT` count drops and gold-hunk hits do not.

---

### 7. `internal/sem/search.go:3188` (`expandSameContainerNeighborCandidates`) — adjacency-only candidates enter the ranking with no query relevance

axum hit **2** is `traits()` at score 27.07, signal `same-container-neighbor` — admitted purely because it is adjacent to hit 1, then re-scored against its own name when the query scores it at zero (`candidate.result.Signals = nil` fallback inside the function). It contributes a body, a rank, and a trailing stray comment line. Gate admission on the neighbor scoring above some fraction of the *query*, not of the seed.

Related, lower value: rank-precision decays hard — ranks 1-2 hit the gold **file** 38.3% of the time, ranks 3-5 12.2%, ranks 6-10 12.7%, ranks 11-22 **4.3%** (232 of 533 entries). Trimming the tail is a clear input-token win (the tail is ~40% of the ranked bytes) but I have **no evidence it reduces output** — eg's Read turns already fell 274 → 189 and its edit count already fell. Rank it as a cache-read saving, not an output one.

---

## Honest caveats

- The eg-q wrapper comment (`tools/eg-q:100-118`) concludes from a *turns* bucketing that "silence is the only outcome that ends the phase," and recommends `EG_VERIFY_MODE=off`. My bucketing of the same 30 sessions by *post-edit output tokens* points the opposite way: silence is the only class that gets worse. Both can be true (fewer turns, each more expensive). For the stated target — output tokens at ~50× a cache-read token — the output bucketing is the one that prices the bill, but this conflict should be settled by one paired cell before `EG_VERIFY_MODE=off` ships.
- Class assignment is not randomised: parse-check repos are interpreted-language repos. I checked the obvious confound (the "none" bucket has the *lowest* baseline post-edit cost per instance, 6.1k vs 9.0k), which cuts against the confound rather than for it, but n=8.
- The shipped top-k raise 10 → 20 is what pulled ranked tests into `subject.testPath` on fastlane and lucene and silently deleted their VERIFY lines; "(NO VERIFY)" went from 8/30 in the recorded run to **11/30** with the current binary. Fix #1 is a regression repair, not a new feature.

All replay artefacts are in `/tmp/eg-agenthunt/replay16/*.txt` (30 payloads from `/tmp/eg-f16` against `replay-wt/`, `--top-k 20`), reproducible in ~4 minutes with the warm caches in `.eg_cache_replay/`.</result>

The two instances that kept their parse check were the two biggest post-edit wins in the benchmark (fastlane −83%, carbon −46%), and my change deleted both.

It also falsifies my own "more sites → more edits" hypothesis: eg made **fewer** edits (70 vs 75) and zero came from RELATED-SITES-only files.

---
name: graph-bench-forensics
description: Measure whether a code-intelligence tool (entire-graph, cmm, any retrieval MCP) actually saves an agent tokens, by reading every session transcript and decomposing tool calls into token cost. Use when benchmarking a tool arm against a no-tool baseline, when a token-savings claim needs verifying or reproducing, or when a measured saving disagrees with a previous result.
---

# Graph benchmark forensics

Measure a context tool honestly, at the level of individual sessions and individual token classes.
This drill exists because aggregates on this benchmark are routinely wrong in *both* directions, and
every headline that was ever withdrawn was withdrawn for a reason this checklist catches.

## The cost model — get this right first, everything else follows

**Cost is not "tokens".** Solve for per-token prices from recorded `total_cost_usd` (least squares
over cache_read / cache_creation / output, n≈30) rather than assuming. Measured on rep30:

| model | $/Mtok cache_read | cache_creation | output | **cost share** cr / cc / out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fable 5 | 1.00 | 20.31 | 49.63 | 22% / 39% / 39% |
| Opus 5 | 0.50 | 10.19 | 24.73 | 26% / 38% / 36% |
| Sonnet | 0.29 | 6.33 | 14.78 | 41% / 31% / 28% |
| Haiku | 0.10 | 2.09 | 4.96 | 46% / 28% / 25% |

Two traps, both of which produced wrong conclusions:

- **"95% of tokens are cache_read" is a token COUNT, not a cost share.** Output is priced 20–50×
  higher, so it is 25–39% of the bill. A tool that cuts reading and raises writing LOSES money.
  Fable is the clean case: turns fell 10% and cost rose 15%, because output rose 14.7%.
- **Cost ≈ MESSAGES × context.** At a large context a message costs ~446k cache-read tokens. Count
  messages, not tool calls. (Note: parallel tool calls were not reachable in this harness — 0 of
  10,374 messages carried more than one — so "batch your calls" is un-actionable advice, and any
  prompt rule telling an agent to batch is dead weight given to both arms.)

Always report cache_read / cache_creation / output **separately**. The aggregate usd hides which
one moved, and which one moved is the finding.

## The noise floor — respect it or you will publish noise

- Same-instance spread across repeated cells: **45pt median**, tail to 335pt. One instance measured
  +404% / +97% / +69% across three configs.
- Every single-cell CI on this benchmark spans zero for the weaker models. **MDE ≈ CI width ≈ 31%
  at n=30**, so only effects ≥ ~30pt are detectable in one cell.
- **0/30 instances produce the same agent query twice** (median token overlap 0.55). Retrieval
  itself varies run to run, so any replay that fixes the query measures one sample of the input.

Rules that follow:
1. **Never score a partial cell.** A Sonnet geomean moved 47 points between n=9 and n=25.
2. **Never bucket one cell into sub-groups of 3–7 and read the differences.** That is how the
   "VERIFY-off is a −12pt lever" and "payload width costs 10.6pt" claims were produced, and both
   were retracted.
3. **Compare configs with replicates of the SAME config**, not two different configs' point
   estimates. Pooling different configs estimates "expected value across configs tried".
4. **Report bootstrap CIs, never a bare point estimate.**
5. Trust **deterministic offline replays** (re-issuing recorded queries against the binary) far
   more than single-session attributions.

## The measurement gate

A session counts only if `total_cost_usd > 0` **AND** `patch.diff` is non-empty. Drop pairs
**symmetrically** — if either arm gate-fails on an instance, the instance leaves both arms.
Otherwise a cheap gate-failure reads as a saving.

Also check before trusting any per-instance delta: `result` length, `num_turns`, and `subtype`
(`error_max_turns` sessions are right-censored, so their true cost is ≥ recorded).

## Fairness — the failure mode that has invalidated the most results

Every withdrawn headline on this benchmark came from **asymmetric prompts**, not from the tool.

- Diff the two arms' `prompt.txt` and account for **every** differing line. A "−35%" result once
  came from two extra instructions the tool arm had and the baseline did not (*"never write a
  throwaway test script"*, *"no `which`, no `ls vendor/`, no `find / -name php*`"*). Removing them
  moved the same cell from −14.9% to +9.1%.
- Frugality clamps belong in the **shared** block or nowhere.
- A tool-side default change (ranking, payload content, a flag) is legitimate. Extra *instructions*
  to one arm are not.
- Distinguish "tool as shipped, including its recommended prompt" from "the tool's marginal value
  under one contract". Both are real questions; say which you measured.

## The drill

### 1. Verify the data before analysing it
- Confirm inputs exist: repo clones, graphs, and **`patch.diff` for every gated session**.
- Check for silent loss: a driver that skips on the session log alone will skip forever a session
  whose patch vanished. On this suite a `/private/tmp` reap destroyed 4 patches, 27 graphs and
  every packfile — and the lost instances were ones the tool won by 20+ turns, biasing *against* it.
- Keep the suite off volatile paths.

### 2. Score the cell
Per-instance paired table: usd, turns, cache_read/cache_creation/output, gate status. Then geomean
+ bootstrap CI. Then per-language, then per-instance sorted by contribution to the shortfall.

### 3. Decompose the transcripts — this is where the answers are
For each session (`~/.claude/projects/*/<session_id>.jsonl`, keyed off `cc_out.json:session_id`):

- **Phase split at the first Edit/Write.** Post-edit is typically ~65% of output and is where every
  losing instance's delta lives.
- **Per-tool token attribution.** Dedupe by `message.id`, credit each message's `output_tokens` to
  its tool. This tells you whether the delta is Edit bodies, Bash commands, or prose.
- **Count**: Edit/Write calls, distinct files touched, throwaway/repro scripts, prose length.
- **Classify every grep/find/read** the tool arm still ran (see below).

### 4. The single strongest predictor found: grep elimination
Compute `eg_greps / baseline_greps` per instance.

| greps eliminated | Haiku | Sonnet |
|---|---|---|
| >75% | **−46.1%** | — |
| 40–75% | −39.6% | −17.3% |
| <40% | +1.9% | +31.8% |

corr(grep ratio, log usd) = **+0.615 Haiku / +0.712 Sonnet**, while corr(**baseline** greps,
outcome) ≈ 0 — so it is not task difficulty leaking through. **This is the metric to optimise.**

Then classify the *residual* greps to decide what to fix:

| what the grep was for | share | fix |
|---|---|---|
| finding something NEW | 38% | recall / ranking |
| searching inside a file the payload returned | 29% | payload under-delivery |
| re-finding a symbol the payload already gave | 25% | payload under-delivery |
| env / build hunting | 8% | verify-command quality |

### 5. Falsify offline before spending a cell
Recorded queries live at `results/<tag>/eg/<instance>/gq_calls.log`, emitted payloads at the same
path + `.payload`, worktrees at `replay-wt/<instance>`. Replay against the binary at **zero model
cost** and assert the change does what you claim — *and* that nothing else moved.

Replay across **every** recorded query variant, not one, because the agent rephrases every run.

### 6. Only then run a cell, and pre-register
Write the prediction and its falsification bounds to a file **before** the run. An out-of-sample
prediction that survives is worth more than ten post-hoc explanations. (Worked: Opus predicted
−0.1% from band effects fitted on cells excluding it; measured −0.5%, n=30.)

## Known results — do not re-derive these

- **≥35% is refuted, not unproven.** The favourable CI bound on total tokens is −27.8%
  (`eg-consolidated/AGENTS.md`). Independent rep30 measurement: Haiku −24.1% CI [−36.6, −8.3].
- Four models, rep30, paired: Fable +14.9%, Opus −0.5%, Sonnet +9.4%, Haiku −24.1%. **The tool
  saves on one of four.**
- Savings depend on how much the *no-tool* arm explores: pooled n=175, corr −0.238
  [−0.346, −0.134]; costs money under ~12 baseline turns, peaks ≈ −30% at 20–49, tapers above.
  **It does not explain Sonnet** (predicted −14.5%, measured +9.4% — a 24pt miss).
- Raising the turn cap does **not** help — both arms grow proportionally (−24.1% → −21.3%).
- Prefetching the search from the issue text is **dominated**: gold-visible@5 0.567 vs 0.715 for the
  agent's own distilled query, 8 losses to 0 wins. The invocation turn is irreducible.
- Retrieval quality and token savings are **different axes**. A config that improved gold-visible
  0.729 → 0.829 across 167 real queries measured *worse* on tokens.

## Discipline

- Keep an **audit ledger**: every claim tagged solid / moderate / retracted, with its basis. Publish
  the retractions.
- When a result contradicts an earlier one, find the mechanism before believing either.
- Correct memory notes in place when they are falsified; a wrong note propagates.
- **Do not stop at a negative finding.** Every apparent dead end here dissolved one layer down — in

Your question found a real bug I introduced. The test answers it precisely:

**Live `search` is *not* stale.** After injecting 40 lines, it returns `CarbonInterface.php:973` — the correct shifted line. It re-indexes the working tree, so it tracks the agent's own edits.

**But my three new filters are.** `_eganchor`, `_egsiblings` and `_egcallees` all read `GSYM` — the static ndjson dump built at base_commit. After the agent edits, their `name -> path:line` pointers drift. `_eganchor` is worst: it *reads body text from the worktree at those stale line numbers*, so it would print the wrong code as if it were the symbol.

import re
GUARD = '''

def live_line(fp, line, name, wt, window=60):
    """Confirm `name` still occurs at/near `line` in the LIVE worktree; return the true line or None.

    The symbol dump (GSYM) is built once, at the session's base commit, and never updated. `search`
    itself re-indexes the working tree — verified: after injecting 40 lines above a symbol, search
    reported its new line, not its old one — but anything derived from the static dump keeps the
    ORIGINAL line numbers. So once the agent has made its first edit, a pointer taken from the dump
    can be off by however many lines that edit added or removed, and a pointer that is off is worse
    than no pointer: it sends the agent to read or edit the wrong place, which is exactly the failure
    mode grep exists to catch.

    Rather than trust the dump, re-locate the bare name in the live file within +/-`window` lines and
    return where it actually is. If it is not there, emit nothing at all.
    """
    import os
    if not (fp and line and wt):
        return None
    path = os.path.join(wt, fp)
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return None
    bare = (name or '').split('.')[-1].split('::')[-1]
    if not bare:
        return None
    try:
        lines = open(path, errors='replace').read().splitlines()
    except Exception:
        return None
    if 1 <= line <= len(lines) and bare in lines[line - 1]:
        return line
    lo, hi = max(0, line - 1 - window), min(len(lines), line - 1 + window)
    best = None
    for idx in range(lo, hi):
        if bare in lines[idx]:
            if best is None or abs(idx - (line - 1)) < abs(best - (line - 1)):
                best = idx
    return best + 1 if best is not None else None
'''

Guard added and verified — 8 pointers against a clean worktree, still 8 against the shifted one (stale ones re-located rather than emitted wrong).

**Answering your question properly, because it has two halves:**

**Does the graph go stale?** The *search* doesn't — it re-indexes the working tree, so it tracks the agent's own edits (proved: injected 40 lines, search reported `:973` not `:933`). But the **static symbol dump** does, and my three new filters were reading it. So yes — they'd have sent the agent to a line that had moved, and `_eganchor` would have printed the *wrong code* under the right symbol name. Now every pointer is re-located against the live file before it's emitted, or dropped.

**Would the agent then edit in the wrong place?** With grep available — no, it catches it. Without grep — yes, and that's the deeper point: **grep is the agent's correctness fallback when the tool is wrong.** This is exactly what the measured history shows. The old eg-only clamp that banned grep-like fallbacks produced *"zero builds or tests on 22 of 31 paired losses"* and `php-4214` where the tool arm ran `which php`, found nothing, stopped as instructed — while the baseline's single `find` located PHP 8.3.32 and resolved.

So the strategy you set is the right one and I'll hold to it: **never forbid grep in the prompt; make the graph good enough that grep isn't reached for.** Elimination has to be earned by capability, and it has to degrade safely — which is why a stale pointer must be dropped rather than guessed.

Where that leaves the goal: v6 stopped (offline A/B showed ~2 of 30 instances would change — not worth 60 sessions). The honest position is that the three shipped fixes are correct but barely reach *this* sample's queries. The lever with real headroom remains grep elimination — 38% of residual greps are genuine recall misses, and that's where I'll aim next rather than another config permutation.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/suhaan/.claude/skills/graph-bench-forensics

# Graph benchmark forensics

Measure a context tool honestly, at the level of individual sessions and individual token classes.
This drill exists because aggregates on this benchmark are routinely wrong in *both* directions, and
every headline that was ever withdrawn was withdrawn for a reason this checklist catches.

## The cost model — get this right first, everything else follows

**Cost is not "tokens".** Solve for per-token prices from recorded `total_cost_usd` (least squares
over cache_read / cache_creation / output, n≈30) rather than assuming. Measured on rep30:

| model | $/Mtok cache_read | cache_creation | output | **cost share** cr / cc / out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fable 5 | 1.00 | 20.31 | 49.63 | 22% / 39% / 39% |
| Opus 5 | 0.50 | 10.19 | 24.73 | 26% / 38% / 36% |
| Sonnet | 0.29 | 6.33 | 14.78 | 41% / 31% / 28% |
| Haiku | 0.10 | 2.09 | 4.96 | 46% / 28% / 25% |

Two traps, both of which produced wrong conclusions:

- **"95% of tokens are cache_read" is a token COUNT, not a cost share.** Output is priced 20–50×
  higher, so it is 25–39% of the bill. A tool that cuts reading and raises writing LOSES money.
  Fable is the clean case: turns fell 10% and cost rose 15%, because output rose 14.7%.
- **Cost ≈ MESSAGES × context.** At a large context a message costs ~446k cache-read tokens. Count
  messages, not tool calls. (Note: parallel tool calls were not reachable in this harness — 0 of
  10,374 messages carried more than one — so "batch your calls" is un-actionable advice, and any
  prompt rule telling an agent to batch is dead weight given to both arms.)

Always report cache_read / cache_creation / output **separately**. The aggregate usd hides which
one moved, and which one moved is the finding.

## The noise floor — respect it or you will publish noise

- Same-instance spread across repeated cells: **45pt median**, tail to 335pt. One instance measured
  +404% / +97% / +69% across three configs.
- Every single-cell CI on this benchmark spans zero for the weaker models. **MDE ≈ CI width ≈ 31%
  at n=30**, so only effects ≥ ~30pt are detectable in one cell.
- **0/30 instances produce the same agent query twice** (median token overlap 0.55). Retrieval
  itself varies run to run, so any replay that fixes the query measures one sample of the input.

Rules that follow:
1. **Never score a partial cell.** A Sonnet geomean moved 47 points between n=9 and n=25.
2. **Never bucket one cell into sub-groups of 3–7 and read the differences.** That is how the
   "VERIFY-off is a −12pt lever" and "payload width costs 10.6pt" claims were produced, and both
   were retracted.
3. **Compare configs with replicates of the SAME config**, not two different configs' point
   estimates. Pooling different configs estimates "expected value across configs tried".
4. **Report bootstrap CIs, never a bare point estimate.**
5. Trust **deterministic offline replays** (re-issuing recorded queries against the binary) far
   more than single-session attributions.

## The measurement gate

A session counts only if `total_cost_usd > 0` **AND** `patch.diff` is non-empty. Drop pairs
**symmetrically** — if either arm gate-fails on an instance, the instance leaves both arms.
Otherwise a cheap gate-failure reads as a saving.

Also check before trusting any per-instance delta: `result` length, `num_turns`, and `subtype`
(`error_max_turns` sessions are right-censored, so their true cost is ≥ recorded).

## Fairness — the failure mode that has invalidated the most results

Every withdrawn headline on this benchmark came from **asymmetric prompts**, not from the tool.

- Diff the two arms' `prompt.txt` and account for **every** differing line. A "−35%" result once
  came from two extra instructions the tool arm had and the baseline did not (*"never write a
  throwaway test script"*, *"no `which`, no `ls vendor/`, no `find / -name php*`"*). Removing them
  moved the same cell from −14.9% to +9.1%.
- Frugality clamps belong in the **shared** block or nowhere.
- A tool-side default change (ranking, payload content, a flag) is legitimate. Extra *instructions*
  to one arm are not.
- Distinguish "tool as shipped, including its recommended prompt" from "the tool's marginal value
  under one contract". Both are real questions; say which you measured.

## The drill

### 1. Verify the data before analysing it
- Confirm inputs exist: repo clones, graphs, and **`patch.diff` for every gated session**.
- Check for silent loss: a driver that skips on the session log alone will skip forever a session
  whose patch vanished. On this suite a `/private/tmp` reap destroyed 4 patches, 27 graphs and
  every packfile — and the lost instances were ones the tool won by 20+ turns, biasing *against* it.
- Keep the suite off volatile paths.

### 2. Score the cell
Per-instance paired table: usd, turns, cache_read/cache_creation/output, gate status. Then geomean
+ bootstrap CI. Then per-language, then per-instance sorted by contribution to the shortfall.

### 3. Decompose the transcripts — this is where the answers are
For each session (`~/.claude/projects/*/<session_id>.jsonl`, keyed off `cc_out.json:session_id`):

- **Phase split at the first Edit/Write.** Post-edit is typically ~65% of output and is where every
  losing instance's delta lives.
- **Per-tool token attribution.** Dedupe by `message.id`, credit each message's `output_tokens` to
  its tool. This tells you whether the delta is Edit bodies, Bash commands, or prose.
- **Count**: Edit/Write calls, distinct files touched, throwaway/repro scripts, prose length.
- **Classify every grep/find/read** the tool arm still ran (see below).

### 4. The single strongest predictor found: grep elimination
Compute `eg_greps / baseline_greps` per instance.

| greps eliminated | Haiku | Sonnet |
|---|---|---|
| >75% | **−46.1%** | — |
| 40–75% | −39.6% | −17.3% |
| <40% | +1.9% | +31.8% |

corr(grep ratio, log usd) = **+0.615 Haiku / +0.712 Sonnet**, while corr(**baseline** greps,
outcome) ≈ 0 — so it is not task difficulty leaking through. **This is the metric to optimise.**

Then classify the *residual* greps to decide what to fix:

| what the grep was for | share | fix |
|---|---|---|
| finding something NEW | 38% | recall / ranking |
| searching inside a file the payload returned | 29% | payload under-delivery |
| re-finding a symbol the payload already gave | 25% | payload under-delivery |
| env / build hunting | 8% | verify-command quality |

### 5. Falsify offline before spending a cell
Recorded queries live at `results/<tag>/eg/<instance>/gq_calls.log`, emitted payloads at the same
path + `.payload`, worktrees at `replay-wt/<instance>`. Replay against the binary at **zero model
cost** and assert the change does what you claim — *and* that nothing else moved.

Replay across **every** recorded query variant, not one, because the agent rephrases every run.

### 6. Only then run a cell, and pre-register
Write the prediction and its falsification bounds to a file **before** the run. An out-of-sample
prediction that survives is worth more than ten post-hoc explanations. (Worked: Opus predicted
−0.1% from band effects fitted on cells excluding it; measured −0.5%, n=30.)

## Known results — do not re-derive these

- **≥35% is refuted, not unproven.** The favourable CI bound on total tokens is −27.8%
  (`eg-consolidated/AGENTS.md`). Independent rep30 measurement: Haiku −24.1% CI [−36.6, −8.3].
- Four models, rep30, paired: Fable +14.9%, Opus −0.5%, Sonnet +9.4%, Haiku −24.1%. **The tool
  saves on one of four.**
- Savings depend on how much the *no-tool* arm explores: pooled n=175, corr −0.238
  [−0.346, −0.134]; costs money under ~12 baseline turns, peaks ≈ −30% at 20–49, tapers above.
  **It does not explain Sonnet** (predicted −14.5%, measured +9.4% — a 24pt miss).
- Raising the turn cap does **not** help — both arms grow proportionally (−24.1% → −21.3%).
- Prefetching the search from the issue text is **dominated**: gold-visible@5 0.567 vs 0.715 for the
  agent's own distilled query, 8 losses to 0 wins. The invocation turn is irreducible.
- Retrieval quality and token savings are **different axes**. A config that improved gold-visible
  0.729 → 0.829 across 167 real queries measured *worse* on tokens.

## Discipline

- Keep an **audit ledger**: every claim tagged solid / moderate / retracted, with its basis. Publish
  the retractions.
- When a result contradicts an earlier one, find the mechanism before believing either.
- Correct memory notes in place when they are falsified; a wrong note propagates.
- **Do not stop at a negative finding.** Every apparent dead end here dissolved one layer down — in
  the transcripts, the harness, or the tool's source. But going deeper is the way through, not a
  licence to loosen the standard of evidence: report the interval, report what you retracted, and
  say plainly when a target is not reached.

Applying it to what's actually in flight. The skill's step 6 says pre-register **before** the run — v7 is at 2/30 and I haven't looked at any result, so I can still do that honestly. And it surfaces a better test than the one I was going to use:

**The direct test of v7 is verb usage, not usd.** If `def`/`callers`/`impact` stay at zero, the change didn't take — and that's a mechanism check with no noise floor to fight.

**Progress report — v7 is measured, failed, and reverted.**

This is the most informative negative of the session, because it's the only config difference in the whole v2–v7 series that was **statistically distinguishable** — and it went the wrong way:

- **Mechanism worked:** `def` 0→3, `callers` 0→2, in-tool `grep` 12→20. Agents *do* adopt a documented verb.
- **Policy backfired:** shell-grep retention **54% → 93%**, turns 24.9 → 31.8, cell −24.1% → **−5.8%**.

Naming a `grep` verb appears to *license* grepping rather than displace it — the agent stacked tool calls on top of its shell greps instead of substituting them. My hypothesis was exactly backwards, and the pre-registered bound caught it rather than me rationalising it after the fact.

The grep-elimination law held precisely, which is *why* the cell lost: the 6 instances that eliminated 40–75% of baseline greps scored **−31.7%**; the 20 that eliminated <40% scored **+7.6%**.

**The actionable lesson, now written into the harness at the point of change:** capability must arrive **in the payload** — already there, unasked-for — never as a verb menu the agent chooses from. That's a sharper design rule than anything I had before, and it rules out a whole family of "just tell it about X" fixes I'd otherwise have kept trying.

**Standing position on the goal:** F remains the best measured config at −24.1% [−36.4, −8.9]. Seven configs tried; none beats it; one is now proven worse. That is consistent with the repo's own recorded verdict that ≥35% is refuted with a favourable bound of −27.8%.

conversation, so a tool call's true price is the context alive when it fires, not the size of its
own result. This walks each transcript, groups JSONL lines by message.id (Claude Code splits ONE
assistant message across several lines - text on one, tool_use on another, so a naive dedup keeps
the text line and reports every message as prose), and charges each message's cache_read /
cache_creation / output to whatever tool it invoked.

Prices solved from recorded total_cost_usd, Haiku: cr 0.10, cc 2.09, out 4.96 $/Mtok.
"""
import json,re,os,sys,collections,statistics
sys.path.insert(0,'/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/0d4c4262-2100-4779-8745-e855e0a78208/scratchpad')
from trace import IDX
AS='/Users/suhaan/graphmark-bench/agentic-swebench'
P_CR,P_CC,P_OT = .10e-6, 2.09e-6, 4.96e-6
GREP=re.compile(r'\b(grep|rg|ag|ack|find|fd)\b')
TEST=re.compile(r'\b(pytest|go test|cargo|npm|yarn|mvn|gradle|make|rspec|rake|phpunit|jest|tsc|javac|gcc|clang|node --check|ruby -c|php -l|py_compile|python -m)\b')
def classify(nm,cmd):
    if nm in ('Edit','Write','MultiEdit'): return 'edit'
    if nm=='Read': return 'read'
    if nm in ('Grep','Glob'): return 'grep/find'
    if nm=='Bash':
        if 'eg-q.run' in cmd: return 'GRAPH TOOL'
        if GREP.search(cmd): return 'grep/find'
        if TEST.search(cmd): return 'test/build'
        return 'other shell'
    return 'other'
def sessions(tag,arm):
    for i in sorted(os.listdir(f'{AS}/results/{tag}/{arm}')):
        p=f'{AS}/results/{tag}/{arm}/{i}/cc_out.json'
        pd=f'{AS}/results/{tag}/{arm}/{i}/patch.diff'
        if not os.path.exists(p): continue
        try: j=json.load(open(p))
        except Exception: continue
        if not (j.get('total_cost_usd') and os.path.exists(pd) and os.path.getsize(pd)>0): continue
        t=IDX.get(j['session_id'])
        if t: yield i,j,t
def walk(t):
    """message.id -> (usage, kind, order). Content is UNIONED across lines sharing an id."""
    msgs=collections.OrderedDict()
    for line in open(t,errors='replace'):
        try:d=json.loads(line)
        except:continue
        if d.get('type')!='assistant':continue
        m=d.get('message') or {}
        mid=m.get('id') or f'anon{len(msgs)}'
        e=msgs.setdefault(mid,dict(cr=0,cc=0,ot=0,kind=None))
        u=m.get('usage') or {}
        if u:
            e['cr']=max(e['cr'],u.get('cache_read_input_tokens',0))
            e['cc']=max(e['cc'],u.get('cache_creation_input_tokens',0))
            e['ot']=max(e['ot'],u.get('output_tokens',0))
        for c in (m.get('content') or []):
            if isinstance(c,dict) and c.get('type')=='tool_use' and e['kind'] is None:
                e['kind']=classify(c['name'],str((c.get('input') or {}).get('command') or ''))
    return list(msgs.values())
def report(lbl,tag,arm):
    agg=collections.defaultdict(lambda: dict(n=0,cr=0,ot=0,cc=0)); ns=0; pos=collections.defaultdict(list)
    for i,j,t in sessions(tag,arm):
        evs=walk(t); ns+=1
        for idx,e in enumerate(evs):
            k=e['kind'] or 'prose only (no tool)'
            a=agg[k]; a['n']+=1; a['cr']+=e['cr']; a['ot']+=e['ot']; a['cc']+=e['cc']
            pos[k].append(idx/max(1,len(evs)-1))
    tot=sum(a['cr']*P_CR+a['cc']*P_CC+a['ot']*P_OT for a in agg.values())
    print(f'\n=== {lbl}  ({ns} sessions)')
    print(f'  {"tool":22} {"calls":>6} {"/sess":>6} {"$ total":>8} {"$/call":>8} {"% of $":>7} {"when":>6}')
    for k,a in sorted(agg.items(),key=lambda x:-(x[1]['cr']*P_CR+x[1]['cc']*P_CC+x[1]['ot']*P_OT)):
        d=a['cr']*P_CR+a['cc']*P_CC+a['ot']*P_OT
        print(f'  {k:22} {a["n"]:6} {a["n"]/ns:6.1f} {d:8.3f} {d/max(1,a["n"]):8.4f} {100*d/tot:6.1f}% {statistics.mean(pos[k]):6.2f}')
    print(f'  {"TOTAL":22} {sum(a["n"] for a in agg.values()):6} {sum(a["n"] for a in agg.values())/ns:6.1f} {tot:8.3f}')
    return agg,ns,tot

    b=report('BASELINE (no tool)','R30HbaseF','baseline')

        bn,en=b[0][k]['n']/b[1], e[0][k]['n']/e[1]
        bd=(b[0][k]['cr']*P_CR+b[0][k]['cc']*P_CC+b[0][k]['ot']*P_OT)/b[1]
        ed=(e[0][k]['cr']*P_CR+e[0][k]['cc']*P_CC+e[0][k]['ot']*P_OT)/e[1]
        print(f'  {k:22} {en-bn:+12.1f} {ed-bd:+10.4f}')
    print(f'  {"TOTAL":22} {"":12} {e[2]/e[1]-b[2]/b[1]:+10.4f}   (baseline ${b[2]/b[1]:.3f}/sess -> eg ${e[2]/e[1]:.3f}/sess)')

Where the tokens actually go

A per-tool cost breakdown of the one configuration that saves money, against an identical no-tool baseline. The headline finding is an inversion: the token class that dominates the count is not the one that dominates the bill, and the tool's saving comes from a single line item.
