1 · Token count is not cost

Per-token prices solved by least squares over cache_read / cache_creation / output against recorded total_cost_usd (Haiku: 0.10 / 2.09 / 4.96 $ per Mtok). Output costs 50× a cache-read token.

A change that cuts reading while raising writing loses money — measured on Fable, where turns fell 10% and cost rose 15% because output rose 14.7%. Always report the three classes separately; the aggregate hides which one moved.

Baseline $0.2406/session · tool $0.1899 · a −35% result needs $0.1564. Shortfall: $0.0335 per session.

Residual grep spend still inside the tool arm: $0.0472 per session — larger than the shortfall. Stated honestly: this is a 20-point point-estimate gap that is NOT statistically distinguishable — n=10 vs 18, difference in log-ratio +0.249 with a 95% CI of [−0.122, +0.650], which spans zero. It is exactly the small-subgroup reading that produced two retracted claims earlier in this investigation. What makes it worth acting on anyway is that the mechanism is deterministic, not statistical: the cap either fires or it does not, the redirect text is in the source, and the fix is testable offline at zero cost. The capped instances are also slightly easier by baseline turns (31.4 vs 33.3), which cuts against a difficulty confound rather than for it.

7 · What has been ruled out

Seven configurations were measured against this baseline. Only one differed from config F at statistical significance, and it was worse.

changeresultwhy it failed
F — top-k 5, VERIFY on−24.1%best measured; CI [−36.4, −8.9]
wider payload (top-k 20 shown)−12.3%not distinguishable from F
+ anchoring, callee expansion−11.8%not distinguishable from F
fetch-wide / show-narrow−17.5%not distinguishable from F
document the tool's other verbs−5.8%distinguishable — and worse

The last one is the instructive failure. Naming def, callers and grep in the prompt did get uptake — def went 0 → 3 calls, callers 0 → 2, in-tool grep 12 → 20. But shell-grep retention rose from 54% to 93%: the agent stacked tool calls on top of its greps rather than substituting them. Paired difference +0.223, CI [+0.045, +0.403].

Design rule this yields. Capability has to arrive in the payload — already present, unasked-for. Offered as a verb the agent may choose to call, it adds a call instead of replacing one. Advertising a grep verb appears to legitimise grepping as an approach rather than displace it.

Method

  • Gate: a session counts only if total_cost_usd > 0 and patch.diff is non-empty; pairs dropped symmetrically so a cheap gate-failure cannot read as a saving.
  • Per-tool attribution groups transcript lines by message.id before charging — Claude Code splits one assistant message across several JSONL lines, so a naive dedup keeps the text line and reports every message as prose.
  • Prices are solved from recorded costs rather than assumed, per model.
  • Same-instance spread across repeated cells is 45 points median, so single-cell differences below ~30 points are not readable. Every comparison above that is called "distinguishable" carries a bootstrap CI excluding zero.

**This is the deepest finding of the entire investigation.** Agent graph usage is *invariant* to configuration:

| config | n | graph calls | shell greps | reads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **F** (lean: top-k 5) | 30 | 1.70 | **6.93** | 6.30 |
| v3 (fetch32/show6) | 30 | 1.47 | 9.40 | 8.23 |
| v4 (+ anchor + callees) | 30 | 1.33 | 7.97 | 8.00 |
| v5 (+ siblings) | 30 | 1.43 | 8.63 | 7.93 |
| v7 (verbs documented) | 30 | 1.70 | **10.93** | 7.97 |
| v8 (cap 1→3) | 13 | 1.54 | 7.23 | 7.85 |
| baseline | 30 | — | 13.97 | 9.13 |

**Graph calls sit at 1.33–1.70 no matter what I do.** Payload width, anchoring, callee expansion, sibling pointers, documenting verbs, tripling the search budget — none of it moves usage. It's a behavioural constant of ~1.5 calls.

And the ordering is brutal: **F is the leanest config, has the fewest greps (6.93), and is the best result (−24.1%). Every enrichment I added increased greps and made things worse.** v7, the richest, has 10.93 greps and −5.8%.

So my whole approach was backwards — I kept *adding* to the payload, and more payload means more leads to chase.

Recorded. v8 at 15/30, graphify and cmm chained behind it.

**Answering your "the graph is barely used" directly — you were right, but the cause isn't what either of us assumed.**

It's not that the tool is hidden or budget-limited. **The agent calls it ~1.5 times per session no matter what**, across six configurations: payload width, anchoring, callee bodies, sibling pointers, documenting the verbs, tripling the search cap. Nothing moves it. Even v8, which lets the agent search three times instead of one, sits at 1.54.

So "get the agent to use the graph more" is not an available lever. And the ordering is humbling:

**F — the leanest config — has the fewest shell greps (6.93) and the best result (−24.1%). Every enrichment I built this session made it worse.** v7, the richest, hit 10.93 greps and −5.8%.

I've been adding to the payload all night on the theory that more information displaces grepping. The data says the opposite: **more payload means more leads to chase.**

That leaves exactly one lever, and it's narrow: **make the top 5 hits more accurate without adding bulk.** The retrieval fixes are the right shape for that — the `codeLikeSearchWeight` digit bug and constant extraction both raise rank without adding a byte. The payload additions were the wrong shape and I'd revert them all.

**All four arms are in, both other tools verified live (28/29 and 28/30 sessions actually called their wrapper).**

| arm | usd | 95% CI | tool calls | greps | turns |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline (no tool) | — | — | — | 13.11 | 32.6 |
| **entire-graph (F)** | **−24.1%** | [−36.2, −8.8] | **1.57** | 6.61 | 32.6 → **24.9** |
| entire-graph (v8) | −20.9% | [−35.1, −3.7] | 1.41 | 8.11 | → 27.8 |
| entire-graph (v8 replicate) | **−23.4%** | [−34.5, −9.8] | 1.25 | 9.07 | → 29.2 |
| graphify | **+9.6%** | [−4.2, +26.3] | 5.67 | 8.93 | → **38.3** |
| cmm | **+15.2%** | [−2.0, +35.3] | 6.96 | 6.93 | → 35.9 |

**entire-graph is the only one of the three tools that saves money.** And the replicate confirms it: −23.4% vs F's −24.1%.

The reason is exactly the cost model. **cmm cuts grepping just as well as eg** (6.93 vs 6.61) — but it needs **6.96 tool calls** to do it versus eg's **1.57**. Since every call is a message and every message re-reads the whole context, cmm spends more finding the answer than it saves.

---

**Now your question — what these two things actually are:**

**Grepping** is the agent searching by *text*. It runs `grep -rn "MICROSECONDS_PER_SECOND" src/` — scanning every file for a string. It's how you find code when you have no map: guess a word, scan, read what comes back, guess again. The no-tool baseline does this **13.1 times per session**, and each one is a full turn costing ~$0.0077.

**entire-graph** is a precomputed *map* of the code — every function, class, method and constant, with the call relationships between them, parsed ahead of time. The agent asks one question in plain language (*"floating-point precision causes interval parsing to fail"*) and gets back ranked locations **with the actual source already inlined** — no scanning, no follow-up read.

The whole bet is that **one map lookup replaces several text scans**. And that's precisely what the data shows it doing:

| | baseline | entire-graph |
|---|---|---|
| greps | 13.11 | 6.61 |
| tool calls | 0 | 1.57 |
| **turns** | **32.6** | **24.9** |

One graph call kills ~6.5 greps. That trade is the entire product, and it's the only line item that moves — edits and test/build are unchanged.

It also explains why the tool fails when it fails: on the 8 instances where the map doesn't contain the answer, the agent greps anyway *and* has paid for the lookup, so it scores −7.7% instead of −30%.

**Confirming Haiku:** −24.1% raw, **−24.9% per resolved issue**, with accuracy slightly *up* (16 resolved vs 15). That's the ceiling — and the arithmetic says why: even perfect retrieval tops out at −29.8%, because the 8 instances the tool can't retrieve still save 7.7% and the 20 it can average −29.8%.

**Launched:** Sonnet eg (its clean baseline already exists), then Opus baseline + eg — best config F, `eg-f18`, eg vs baseline only, prompt verified free of the contamination I found earlier.

**Grading delegated to a subagent** so it doesn't block us — it'll do graphify and cmm, plus cost-per-resolved.

While that runs, the four-arm token composition explains the earlier result cleanly:

| | baseline | entire-graph | graphify | cmm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the tool | — | **1.6 · $0.015** | 5.7 · $0.042 | 7.5 · $0.075 |
| grep/find | 13.1 · $0.101 | **6.4 · $0.047** | 8.9 · $0.061 | 6.7 · $0.053 |
| read | 8.4 · $0.056 | **6.2 · $0.045** | 9.5 · $0.064 | 7.7 · $0.066 |
| **total** | **$0.2405** | **$0.1891** | $0.2815 | $0.3298 |

**cmm cuts grepping about as well as entire-graph (6.7 vs 6.4) but spends 7.5 tool calls doing it instead of 1.6** — so it pays $0.075 to save $0.048. graphify is the same shape. entire-graph wins because it answers in one call, not because it answers better.

One caveat on the accuracy numbers: 1-resolve differences at n=27 aren't significant. The defensible claim is *accuracy flat, cost down*.

Where the baseline greps 9.5 times, the tool cuts that to 5.4 and cuts writing 30%. Where the baseline greps 5.8 times, there is nothing to save and the added context doubles the model's output.

# Sonnet: −20% suite-wide by removing the "don't re-read" prohibition

## Context

`entire-graph` (eg) saves money on Haiku (−24.1% CI [−36.6, −8.8], accuracy tied 17 vs 16 resolved)
and loses money on Sonnet (**+9.4%**). Five configs have been tried on Sonnet — F, BEST, v9, wide-k,
verify-off — and every one lands between +3.6% and +9.4%. The goal chosen for this plan is
**−20% suite-wide on Sonnet, representative 30-instance sample, no caveats.**

### The arithmetic that rules out the obvious approach

Abstention/gating cannot get there, and this is not a matter of finding a better gate:

```
today, no gate                                     +7.4%
best real gate found (payload dispersion)          -5.4%
PERFECT ORACLE gate — abstain on all 16 losers    -15.8%   <- hard ceiling of ANY gate
```

An abstained instance contributes 0%, not savings. Even a gate with perfect foresight stops at
−15.8%. **−20% therefore requires the losing instances to start winning, not to be skipped.** For
reference, the 14 winners already average −30.9%; if the 16 losers merely reached −10%, the suite
lands at −20.5%.

I also tested the dispersion gate properly before relying on it: pooled across three Sonnet cells the
wide-minus-narrow gap is +12.3% with **95% CI [−11.0, +41.8]** — it does not separate. That
replicates the earlier §3 REFUTED finding. Dispersion gating is dead; it is not in this plan.

## The mechanism (measured, 60 sessions, full transcript attribution)

The loss is **~100% thinking tokens, ~84% of it before the first edit.**

| per-instance mean output | WINNERS (14) base→eg | LOSERS (16) base→eg |
|---|---|---|
| messages containing `thinking` | 9,356 → 6,806 (−2,551) | 6,398 → 15,851 (**+9,453**) |
| `tool_use` only | 1,201 → 404 | 855 → 823 |
| text + `tool_use` | 1,216 → 942 | 1,280 → 1,156 |
| text only | 160 → 221 | 181 → 191 |
| **total** | 11,933 → 8,373 | 8,713 → 18,020 (**+9,307**) |

Thinking-bearing messages are **101.6%** of the loser increase; the other three buckets net −146.
Confirmed independently by `thinking.signature` bytes (losers +126%, winners −26%) and by the
residual after subtracting visible text and tool-input JSON. Split at the first edit: losers
**+7,778 pre-edit** vs +1,530 post; winners −2,802 post-edit vs −758 pre. Mirror images.

### Why: the eg prompt forbids paging state into context

Diffing the emitted `prompt.txt` of both arms (structurally symmetric, baseline's block is *longer*,
both carry the frugality clamp — fairness is fine), the arms are told **opposite** things:

| baseline rule (2) | eg rules (2) and (3) |
|---|---|
| "**READ** the enclosing function of the hit, as one range" | "**Do not re-read** that file. Do not search again to confirm." / "**Do not grep** for either." |

Thinking bills at **$14.78/Mtok**; cache_read bills at **$0.29/Mtok** — a **51× markup**. The
prohibition makes Sonnet substitute the expensive channel for the cheap one. Three transcripts show
it directly:

- **micropython-15898** (+164%) — the only `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` in all 60 sessions.
  Message index 1 is **64,000 output tokens, zero tool calls**, fired the instant search returned,
  before any Read. The payload was the complete 82-line body of `mpz_as_str_inpl` — correct, but
  subtle. The next message is another 10,991 tokens, and then it runs
  `Read py/mpz.c offset=1690 limit=40` **anyway** — the read it was told to skip, 75,000 tokens later.
  Baseline instead externalised the problem: one grep, two Reads, one 7,373-token think, 13,068 total.
- **pylint-7080** (+374%, 14→50 messages) — VERIFY was derived from the **irrelevant rank-4 hit**
  (`test_find_default_config_files`), not from the rank-2 hit it actually edits. It then spent
  messages 28–41 hunting a toolchain (`pyenv versions`, `pip3 index versions py`,
  `python3.10 -m pip install --user py`) and built **six** repro trees before its first edit at
  message 46 of 50. Baseline: edit at message 4, done in 14.
- **hugo-12562** (+241%) — top three hits are thin dispatch wrappers (`Site.GetPage`, 13 lines,
  delegates; `Site.checkReady`, a 5-line panic guard). **The real fix site is absent from the
  payload.** Forced to recover while instructed not to search, it made four successive edits to the
  same file. Baseline reached the same fix in one edit at message 7.

Winners are the mirror: fluentd-4655 (−57%) ran 6 messages, accepted a missing-gem failure and
stopped; valkey-1499 (−57%) **still grepped 5 times** and won anyway. The clean discriminator is
**peak single-message output** — winners 519 / 932 / 697, losers 64,000 / 6,401 / 2,006.

### What is NOT the cause (tested, do not revisit)

Payload shape does not discriminate, and leans the *wrong* way: winners' payloads are **larger**
(4,117 B vs 3,029 B). Numbered hits 5.29 vs 5.31, distinct files 3.93 vs 4.12, has-VERIFY 0.71 vs
0.81. Retrieval quality does not discriminate either: gold present 11/14 vs 12/16, gold at rank 1
5/14 vs 5/16, mean gold rank 1.64 vs 1.75. `RELATED SITES` **never fires anywhere**. Language shows
no signal; repo size leans opposite to the naive guess.

## The work

### 1. Replace the prohibition with baseline's contract (the lever)

In `tools/run_3arm.sh`, eg rules (2) and (3) currently forbid re-reading, re-searching and grepping.
Replace rule (2) with the baseline's own wording — *read the enclosing function of the hit as one
range* — and drop "Do not grep for either" from (3). Keep the search-first ordering and the shared
frugality clamp; the change is only that eg is no longer *forbidden* the cheap channel.

This is a fairness correction, not an arm advantage: it moves eg's contract **toward** baseline's,
and removes text that is uniquely handicapping eg. Edit the heredoc with the known hazard in mind —
shell comments and unquoted backticks inside `cat <<TXT` leak into the emitted prompt (this cost a
full day once). **Verify by diffing the emitted `prompt.txt`, never the source.**

### 2. Derive VERIFY from the hit the agent will edit, or emit nothing

`internal/sem/search_verify.go` currently derives the VERIFY command from build evidence without
binding it to the top-ranked hit — pylint's came from rank 4. Bind derivation to the rank-1
implementation hit; if no test plausibly covers that file, emit nothing. Silence is the block's
documented contract. Also probe the runner (`exec.LookPath` plus the manifest-local paths the deriver
already computes) and stay silent when it is absent, rather than emitting the
"runner is not installed" NOTE that pylint ignored.

### 3. Demote thin delegating wrappers below the implementation they delegate to

Hugo's top three hits were wrappers. In `internal/sem/search.go` scoring, a symbol whose body is
under ~15 lines and whose sole substantive statement is a call to another in-repo symbol should rank
below its callee. The `CALLS` edge needed is already loaded (`_egcallees.py` uses it today).

### 4. Cap the pathological single message

micropython alone plus pylint are **62%** of the loser group's total growth, and micropython breached
`max_tokens` at 64,000 in one message. Whatever §1 achieves, a payload that triggers a 64K
single-message think is a defect. After §1 lands, re-check whether that instance still spikes; if it
does, the payload is over-dense for one turn and should be split across the head hit plus locators.

## Files

- `graphmark-bench/agentic-swebench/tools/run_3arm.sh` — eg rules (2), (3) (§1)
- `eg-consolidated/internal/sem/search_verify.go` — VERIFY binding + runner probe (§2)
- `eg-consolidated/internal/sem/search.go` — wrapper demotion in scoring (§3)

## Verification

1. **Prompt diff first.** Emit one prompt per arm and diff them; account for every differing line.
   Confirm no comment or backtick leaked into the heredoc.
2. **Free offline replay before any spend.** Re-issue the recorded queries in
   `results/*/eg/*/gq_calls.log` against the new binary. Assert: pylint's VERIFY now targets the
   rank-2 file or is silent; hugo's fix site outranks `Site.GetPage`; **and that gold rank does not
   regress on the other 28** — retrieval quality and token savings are different axes, and a config
   that improved gold-visible 0.729→0.829 previously measured *worse* on tokens.
3. `cd /Users/suhaan/devenv/eg-consolidated && mise run check` (2008 tests green today); regression
   tests for §2 silence and §3 ordering.
4. **Pre-register the prediction** to a file before spending: losers' pre-edit thinking falls from
   +7,778 to ≈0; suite lands in [−25%, −12%]. Then run Sonnet eg against the existing `R30SbaseF`
   baseline (reusable — baselines are tool-independent).
5. Score total, geomean, **bootstrap CI**, turns, peak single-message output, and thinking-bearing
   output separately. MDE ≈31% at n=30, so report the interval, never the bare point estimate.
6. If the point estimate clears −20% but the CI spans it, run a **replicate of the same config** —
   not a different config — before claiming the number.

## Honest expectation

The arithmetic works only if the losers convert from positive to roughly −10%. §1 addresses the
measured cause of ~100% of their excess, so this is the best-supported shot available — but the
mechanism is established on 30 sessions with two instances contributing 62% of the effect, and the
remaining 14 losers show a milder version (thinking blocks +43%, output +46%) rather than a
catastrophe. A plausible outcome is that Sonnet lands between −5% and −15%: a real, defensible
improvement that still misses −20%. I will report the interval and say plainly if the target is not
reached rather than reframing the claim.

## Rules held throughout

- No model-name branching in the tool.
- No arm-advantaging prompt text. §1 only *removes* a handicap; verify by diffing emitted prompts.
- Never score a partial cell; drop gate-failing pairs symmetrically from both arms.
- Report cache_read / cache_creation / output separately — the aggregate hides which one moved.

Losers' output rose +9,307 tok/instance, of which thinking-bearing messages are 101.6% and 84% is
pre-edit. Thinking bills at $14.78/Mtok against cache_read's $0.29/Mtok. The claim is that the
prohibition made Sonnet substitute the 51×-more-expensive channel for the cheap one.

Summary of what happened, including two things I got wrong:

**Shipping §1 only.** The eg arm was handicapped relative to baseline — told *"Do not re-read that file. Do not search again… Do not grep for either,"* while baseline was told *"READ the enclosing function"* and *"grep the distinctive literal once more."* That's the measured cause: **101.6% of the losing instances' excess output is thinking tokens, 84% of it pre-edit**, and thinking bills at **$14.78/Mtok vs cache_read's $0.29 — a 51× premium**. The prohibition forced Sonnet to hold the file in its head instead of in context. eg now has baseline's affordances and zero residual eg-only prohibitions.

**§2 was built, replayed, and reverted — I was wrong twice:**

1. **I misattributed the cause.** I claimed pylint-7080's bad VERIFY came from the ranked-test path. It came from the *covering-test* path (`derived_from` says so plainly). My gate guarded code that wasn't the problem.
2. **My core premise was false.** I assumed rank-1 is the fix site. In fluentd the agent edited `lib/fluent/plugin/in_http.rb` while rank-1 was a different file — the covering-test block is often better evidence of the fix site than rank is. Extending the gate degraded real test commands to parse checks **on known winners**: fluentd (−57%), nushell (−62%), preact.

The free offline replay caught both before a cent was spent. That's what it's for. Tool source is back at clean HEAD, `internal/sem` green.

**Binary is `eg-f18`** — the same build `R30SegF` and `R30SegBEST` used — so v10 differs from them by the prompt and nothing else. Clean attribution.

**On the graph question you raised:** it surfaced a genuine defect — Go `var`/`const` are not indexed as symbols at all (`variable: 0, constant: 0`), so `def lowConfidenceTopScore` returns nothing and you must grep. But I over-claimed its impact and the measurement corrected me: **3% of eg-arm greps**, and 4 of those 5 were functions my regex mis-matched. Worth filing, not a lever.

Pre-registered in `PREDICTION-v10.md`: primary is **P4, suite geomean in [−25%, −12%], falsified if it lands above 0%**. If it lands positive I'll report the mechanism as wrong rather than reaching for a sixth config. ETA ~40–60 min for 30 sessions at CONC=4.

saves suite-wide and Sonnet does not.

| config | base<20 | base>=20 |
|---|---|---|
| F / v9 (lean, k=5) | **+24.0% / +19.7%** | −5.3% / −5.2% |
| BEST / v10 (rich) | +38.0% / +40.9% | **−19.4% / −17.2%** |

Lean wins easy tasks, rich wins hard ones. **An ORACLE picking the best config per instance still
gives only −0.5% suite-wide.** Combined with the oracle-abstention ceiling of −15.8%
([[sonnet-loss-is-conserved]]), suite-wide −25% on rep30/Sonnet is unreachable — it needs the easy
band to swing 67 points.

## Where Sonnet actually slacks (post-payload tool calls, n=30 sessions, 546 calls)

35.9% build/test/repro · 31.5% grep for something NEW · 12.5% edit · 10.1% re-read a payload file ·
8.8% read a new file · 1.3% grep for text the payload had. Only **11.4% is redundant** with the
payload, so the payload is not the waste.

(5.70 → 4.83) vs Haiku's ~47%. **67% of the residual greps are declaration hunting** — the agent does

`ResolvedPythonType\|PythonType`, `class tuple_join\|struct tuple_join\|tuple_join_format`,

1. Oracle *abstention* (skip all 16 losers, keep all 14 winners) → **−15.8%** ceiling

This table is the answer to "where exactly is it going wrong." Look at the grep column:

**Every loser has *negative* elimination — eg makes Sonnet grep MORE than no tool at all:**
```
hugo         4 -> 19.3 greps  (-383%)  turns 12 -> 42.7   gold MISS   cost +317%
immutable-js 3 ->  7.0        (-133%)                     gold r2     cost  +57%
pylint       3 ->  6.7        (-122%)                     gold r1     cost  +45%
```
**Every winner has high elimination:**
```
fluentd      5 ->  1.3        (+73%)   turns 21 -> 11.3               cost  -35%
valkey      14 ->  6.3        (+55%)   turns 27 -> 14.3               cost  -47%
redis        4 ->  2.0        (+50%)                                  cost  -42%
```

And `tests@5` is 0/5 nearly everywhere, so test-pollution isn't it. The induced grepping concentrates on **gold MISS** — the payload shows 5 confident-looking wrong candidates and sends the agent hunting. Testing whether a miss is *detectable* at emit time, which is the fix:

**A detector exists.** Lexical density — the fraction of repo symbols the query's words actually match — separates misses with high precision:

```
dens < 0.322   catches 4/8 misses,  1/22 false alarms
gap12 < 0.008  catches 4/8 misses,  2/22 false alarms

But look at the gold-**HIT** losers, because they reveal the real pathology:

```
gson-2158    gold r2   greps 9->9.3   reads 1->5.3   turns 17 -> 29.3   +80%
immutable-js gold r2   greps 3->7.0                  turns 10 -> 18.3   +57%
pylint       gold r1   greps 3->6.7                  turns 14 -> 25.0   +45%
```

**eg finds the answer and Sonnet still nearly doubles its turns.** The payload doesn't just fail to help — five ranked candidates with complete bodies *invite investigation*. The baseline, given nothing, greps one literal and edits. That's confirmed by the config table: the richer payload (BEST) is worse on the easy band (+38.0%) than the lean one (F, +24.0%), and better on the hard band (−19.4% vs −5.3%).

**So the two bands want opposite payloads, and I can now detect which band I'm in.** Implementing that as a tool-side tier:

**Definitive.** Every gold hit in the entire sample is at rank 1, 2, or 3:

```

Ranks 4–5 buy **nothing** in recall and cost pure investigation surface — which is exactly what makes Sonnet grep 3→7 and double its turns on easy tasks. And at k=12 the 3 recoverable misses sit at ranks 6–12. So the optimal shape is **top-3 when confident, wide only when the top-3 likely missed.** Building that tier into the wrapper's tested block logic:

# CONFIDENCE TIER (EG_CONF_TIER=1). Measured on 30 recorded rep30 payloads: EVERY gold file that the

# against the no-tool arm (hugo 4->19.3, immutable-js 3->7.0, pylint 3->6.7) and turns roughly double
# even when gold WAS found at rank 1-2 (gson-2158 17->29.3 turns at gold rank 2).
#
# But narrowing unconditionally would give up the one case where depth pays: when the top-3 MISSED,
# widening to 12 recovers gold on 3 of 8 misses (22/30 -> 25/30) with zero displacement. So the width
# is chosen per query from a signal the ranker already has -- the relative score gap between hit 1 and
# hit 2. A near-zero gap means the ranking did not actually discriminate.
#   gap >= EG_CONF_GAP  -> CONFIDENT -> show EG_CONF_NARROW (3). Costs 0 gold at every threshold tried.
#   gap <  EG_CONF_GAP  -> weak      -> show everything fetched, and say so.
CONF_TIER   = os.environ.get("EG_CONF_TIER", "0") == "1"
CONF_GAP    = float(os.environ.get("EG_CONF_GAP", "0.008"))
CONF_NARROW = int(os.environ.get("EG_CONF_NARROW", "3"))''')

s=s.replace('''out = []
n = 0
per_file = {}''',

        return float(m.group(1)) if m else 0.0
    s1, s2 = _score(blocks[0]), _score(blocks[1])
    gap = (s1 - s2) / s1 if s1 > 0 else 0.0

I went deep into the transcripts and per-repo tool usage as you asked, and it produced a concrete tool change. Here's exactly where it's slacking:

**Per-repo, the losers all share one signature — eg makes Sonnet grep *more* than using no tool at all:**

```
hugo          4 -> 19.3 greps  (-383%)   turns 12 -> 42.7   gold MISS   +317%
immutable-js  3 ->  7.0        (-133%)   turns 10 -> 18.3   gold r2      +57%

gson-2158     9 ->  9.3          (-4%)   turns 17 -> 29.3   gold r2      +80%
```
versus winners: fluentd +73% elimination (−35%), valkey +55% (−47%), redis +50% (−42%).

Note `gson-2158`: **gold found at rank 2, and Sonnet still nearly doubled its turns.** So it's not a retrieval failure — the payload itself is inviting investigation.

**Then the measurement that explains it.** Across all 30 payloads, every gold file the tool found sat at rank 1, 2, or 3:

```
gold ranks found: [1×10, 2×9, 3×3]
gold at rank 4 or 5:  ZERO
```

**Ranks 4–5 buy no recall whatsoever.** They're pure investigation surface, and Sonnet spends turns on them. That's confirmed independently by the config table — the richer payload is worse on easy tasks (+38.0% vs lean's +24.0%) and better on hard ones (−19.4% vs −5.3%).

**The change, now built and validated:** a confidence tier keyed on the hit-1/hit-2 score gap the ranker already computes. Discriminating ranking → show 3. Non-discriminating → show 12 and say so. On all 30 recorded payloads: **25 narrowed, 5 warned, gold preserved 22/22**, and the warning fires on hugo (+317%), lucene (+56%), laravel (+35%).

Widening alone recovers 3 of the 8 misses (22→25/30) at ranks 6–12, so the wide branch is earned too.

**v11 is a clean negative — and it confirms the mechanism precisely.** Uniform widening makes things worse overall while splitting exactly as the theory predicts:

```

F    k=5      +9.9%      +22.1%        -3.5%      20.0

Width **helps the hard band** (−14.7% vs F's −3.5%) and **badly hurts the easy band** (+53.5% vs +22.1%). That is the investigation-surface effect in isolation: extra hits with no recall value cost 4 turns and 31 points on tasks that didn't need them.

I have to own that this refutes my own reasoning from two steps ago — I argued from offline recall (22→25/30 gold recovered) that widening should help. Recall improved and cost got *worse*. That's the "retrieval quality and token savings are different axes" law biting again, and it's why I ran the cell instead of shipping k=12 on the offline number.

**It also validates the v13 tier design directly**: the two bands demonstrably want opposite widths, and v13 gives each what it wants — narrow-3 when the ranking discriminated, wide-12 plus a warning when it didn't.

---
name: eg-confidence-tier
description: Payload width should be chosen per query from the hit1/hit2 score gap — narrow 3 when the ranking discriminated, wide 12 + warning when it did not; best Sonnet config measured
metadata:
  type: project
---

MEASURED 2026-08-01, rep30/Sonnet, common gated subset n=26, vs `R30SbaseF`.

| config | suite | base<20 | base>=20 | turns |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F k=5 | +7.6% | +21.1% | −6.2% | 19.6 |
| BEST k=5 | +8.1% | +37.5% | −18.3% | 19.8 |
| v11 k=12 uniform | +24.4% | +58.9% | −6.5% | 24.8 |
| **v13 TIER 3/12** | **−0.6%** | **+17.9%** | **−18.6%** | 20.7 |
| baseline | — | — | — | 19.4 |

The tier is the **best config in BOTH bands at once** — it beats the lean payload on easy tasks and the
wide payload on hard ones. Paired against F on the same instances: **−7.7%, CI [−22.1, +9.7]**,
cheaper on 15/26. Promising, not proven, at n=26.

## The finding it is built on

Across 30 recorded rep30 payloads, EVERY gold file the payload contained sat at rank 1, 2 or 3 —
observed rank multiset **[1×10, 2×9, 3×3]**, and ranks 4–5 held gold **zero** times. The tail buys no
recall; it buys investigation surface, and Sonnet spends it. On losing instances greps go UP versus
the no-tool arm (hugo 4→19.3, immutable-js 3→7.0, pylint 3→6.7) and turns roughly double even when
gold WAS found at rank 1–2 (gson-2158: gold r2, turns 17→29.3).

Widening is not free either — v11 (uniform k=12) measured **+24.4%**, worse than k=5, because the
easy band went to +58.9%. Width helps only where recall is actually missing: widening recovers gold
on 3 of 8 misses (22→25/30), all at ranks 6–12.

## The rule

Width is chosen per query from the **relative score gap between hit 1 and hit 2**, which the ranker
already computes:
- `gap >= 0.008` → discriminating → show **3**. Costs 0 gold at every threshold tried.
- `gap < 0.008` → show everything fetched (12) **and say so** in a LOW CONFIDENCE line.

Offline on all 30 recorded payloads: 25 narrowed, 5 warned, **gold preserved 22/22**. Live in the
cell: 8/11 narrowed, and the warning fires on hugo-12562 (+317%), lucene (+56%), laravel (+35%).

Implemented in `agentic-swebench/tools/_egsearch.py` behind `EG_CONF_TIER=1` /`EG_CONF_GAP` /
`EG_CONF_NARROW`. **Two silent-failure traps:** `tools/eg-q`'s `_pp()` only runs the post-filter for a
whitelist of flags (had to add `EG_CONF_TIER`), and `run_3arm.sh`'s env line must pass the new vars or
they never reach the wrapper. Either one makes the cell measure nothing while looking like it ran —
always verify by counting ranked hits in an emitted payload, and count ONLY the block before the
first section header (`RELATED SITES`/`DOCS & FIXTURES` also emit numbered lines).

## Not yet ported to the tool

This lives in the benchmark wrapper. The Go equivalent belongs in `internal/sem/search.go`, where
both signals are native (`lexical_candidates`/`symbols_considered` give a density signal too, which
catches 4/8 misses with 1/22 false alarms). `AssessSearchConfidence` currently keys on an absolute
top-score ceiling of 12.0 while the observed minimum is 20.3, which is why LOW CONFIDENCE never
fires. Recalibrate it onto the **gap**, not the absolute score. Do NOT calibrate it on cost — payload
features do not predict cost ([[sonnet-band-structure]]); calibrate on MISS prediction, which works.

2. No confirmation of char-for-char match against the live working tree (search results could in principle be from a stale cache). Same Read call (#3) also served this purpose.
3. Nothing else was missing — the rest of the payload (related sites, covering tests, verify command) was more than adequate and unused mostly because the task said not to run the build.

## 4. WHY WAS THE GREP PATH CHEAPER

One `grep -n "sentenceStarts.length / 2"` would have returned exactly one line: `135:      currentSentence = sentenceStarts.length / 2; // start search from the middle` (or similar with the real line number), directly answering "where" and "what line" in one shot, zero ambiguity, minimal tokens.

The search payload gave far more: both the buggy method AND its correct sibling AND covering tests AND related sibling classes AND a same-literal census AND a verify command — genuinely useful context (confirms correct replacement text, confirms no other call sites need the same fix) that grep would not have surfaced. But for the narrow "find and fix one line" task, that's a lot of payload weight (10+ hits, ~80 lines of text) versus grep's single line. Honestly: grep is cheaper to eyeball; the search tool is more thorough but heavier. Given the fix was genuinely two near-identical functions, the search payload's inclusion of the sibling `following` method was worth more than grep alone would give (grep for the literal wouldn't have shown me the correct pattern to copy — I'd have had to derive `(length-1)/2` myself, or grep separately for `following`). So it's a wash on call count (both got me there in effectively 1 useful lookup + 1 edit) but grep is lighter weight per call, while search de-risked "did I copy the right replacement" for free.

Should the tool have just shown the literal's occurrences? For a "fix this exact reported line" issue with a literal quoted verbatim in the report, yes — a literal-occurrence view (like grep -n but symbol-boundary-aware) as a fast-path alongside the semantic ranking would let an agent verify-and-edit in one glance rather than parsing method bodies to find the token.

## 5. THE ONE CHANGE

Add a line-precise pointer to the specific matched token/line within each complete-symbol hit, not just the enclosing method's start-end range — e.g., when the query text or issue contains a literal code fragment, annotate the hit with `matched_line=151` (or bold/mark the matching line inside the printed body) so the agent can act without a follow-up Read to confirm the exact line number for the Edit's old_string anchor. export const meta = {
  name: 'opus-reach-25pct',
  description: 'Forensics on every Opus benchmark cell, then implement + verify fixes on a dedicated branch',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Forensics', detail: 'four independent reads of the Opus cells' },
    { title: 'Synthesise', detail: 'rank defects by measured impact, pick what to build' },
    { title: 'Implement', detail: 'one worktree-isolated agent per accepted defect' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'build, tests, and free offline replay' },
  ],
}

const REPO = args.repo
const SUITE = args.suite
const EG = args.opus_eg_cells.join(' ')
const BASE = args.opus_base_cells.join(' ')

const GROUND = `
GROUND TRUTH you must not re-derive (measured this session, trust it):
- Cost = billed total_cost_usd. Gate every session on total_cost_usd>0 AND non-empty patch.diff; drop
  pairs symmetrically. Never score a partial cell. Report bootstrap CIs, never a bare point estimate.
  Minimum detectable effect is ~31% at n=30, so ignore differences smaller than that in ONE cell.
- Opus today: R30Oeg -2.9% CI [-10.8,+5.7]; R30OegBEST +7.2%. Haiku -25.0% CI [-32.2,-17.0]. Sonnet
  best config -2.2%.
- THE BAND LAW (measured on Sonnet, n=89 runs): the tool's outcome is a step function of how much the
  NO-TOOL baseline explores. baseline>=20 turns -> -14.1% CI [-22.7,-4.7]; baseline<20 -> +34.1% CI
  [+15.5,+55.5]. corr(baseline turns, cost) = -0.494. Opus's baseline runs ~12.8 turns, i.e. entirely
  inside the losing band. Any proposal must confront this.
- Gold-file rank: across 149 real payloads from Haiku and Sonnet, 97.7%/98.4% of all gold the payload
  contained sat at rank 1-3; ranks 4-5 held gold once in 105 found cases.
- NO static payload feature predicts a retrieval miss: AUC 0.563 gap, 0.553 top score, 0.560 spread,
  0.690 entropy, at a 28% base rate. Do not propose a threshold on payload features.
- Naming a graph verb in the prompt BACKFIRES (measured 3x: v7, and v14 = v13 + one line naming 'def'
  went -0.6% -> +14.9%). Prompt text is not a lever. Tool-side changes only.
- Uniform widening is worse: k=12 measured +18.9% vs k=5 +9.4% on Sonnet.
- Transcripts: results/<cell>/<arm>/<iid>/cc_out.json carries session_id; resolve it with
  /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/0d4c4262-2100-4779-8745-e855e0a78208/scratchpad/trace.py
  (import IDX; IDX[session_id] -> transcript path). Payloads: same dir + gq_calls.log.payload.
- Use ${SUITE}/.venv/bin/python for analysis.
OUTPUT STYLE: compressed. Numbers and file:line, not prose. No preamble, no summary of the task.
`

phase('Forensics')
const LENSES = [
  { key: 'phases', prompt: `Phase-split every Opus session in cells ${EG} against baselines ${BASE} in ${SUITE}.
For each session classify every assistant tool call as locate(grep/find/ls/cat) / read / edit / build / other,
split at the FIRST Edit/Write. Report per-arm means: pre-edit locate, pre-edit read, post-edit explore,
build, total. Then the SAME table for Haiku (${args.haiku_ref.join(' vs ')}) as contrast.
Answer precisely: how many calls of the Opus baseline are pre-edit locate, and therefore what is the
arithmetic CEILING for a locate tool that costs one call of its own? Give the number.` },
  { key: 'perrepo', prompt: `Per-repo and per-language forensics for Opus, cells ${EG} vs ${BASE} in ${SUITE}.
Language/repo come from ${SUITE}/tasks/rep30_tasks.json. For every repo report: cost ratio (geomean over
cells), baseline greps -> eg greps and the elimination %, baseline turns -> eg turns, and the gold-file
rank in the emitted payload. Sort worst-to-best. Then state which repos lose, whether losing repos share
a language, a size, or a baseline-turn range, and quantify with a correlation.` },
  { key: 'coverage', prompt: `For Opus cells ${EG} in ${SUITE}: what fraction of the BASELINE's pre-edit locate work
does the eg payload already answer? For every baseline pre-edit grep/Read, decide whether the emitted
payload (gq_calls.log.payload) already contained that file or that literal. Report answered vs not, split
by grep versus Read. Then for the greps it does NOT cover, classify where the searched literal came from:
present in the issue text (tasks json problem_statement), present in the agent's own query (first line of
gq_calls.log), or invented by the agent mid-session. Give percentages.` },
  { key: 'deepread', prompt: `Read the actual transcripts of the FIVE worst Opus instances by cost ratio (cells ${EG}
vs ${BASE} in ${SUITE}) and the THREE best. For each, give a numbered call-by-call trace of the eg arm and
the baseline arm side by side, and name the exact turn where the eg arm diverged and started costing more.
Quote real commands. Then state, per instance, the single change to the RETURNED PAYLOAD that would have
prevented the divergence. Be concrete about the output format wanted.` },
]

const FIND = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['headline', 'numbers', 'defects'],
  properties: {
    headline: { type: 'string', description: 'one sentence, the single most important measured fact' },
    numbers: { type: 'string', description: 'the tables/figures, compressed, with n and CIs' },
    defects: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        required: ['defect', 'evidence', 'est_impact_pct', 'fix'],
        properties: {
          defect: { type: 'string' },
          evidence: { type: 'string', description: 'the measurement, with n' },
          est_impact_pct: { type: 'number', description: 'estimated pp of suite cost this could recover; be conservative' },
          fix: { type: 'string', description: 'concrete tool-side change, name the file' },
        },
      },
    },
  },
}

const findings = await parallel(LENSES.map(l => () =>
  agent(`${GROUND}\n\nTASK (${l.key}):\n${l.prompt}`,
        { label: `forensics:${l.key}`, phase: 'Forensics', schema: FIND })))

phase('Synthesise')
const valid = findings.filter(Boolean)
log(`${valid.length}/4 lenses returned; ${valid.reduce((n, f) => n + (f.defects || []).length, 0)} candidate defects`)

const PLAN = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['verdict', 'accepted', 'rejected'],
  properties: {
    verdict: { type: 'string', description: 'is 25% reachable on Opus, and under what condition; state plainly if not' },
    accepted: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        required: ['title', 'file', 'change', 'why', 'risk_to_haiku', 'offline_test'],
        properties: {
          title: { type: 'string' }, file: { type: 'string' },
          change: { type: 'string', description: 'precise, implementable' },
          why: { type: 'string', description: 'the measurement that justifies it' },
          risk_to_haiku: { type: 'string', description: 'how this could cost Haiku its -25%, and how to bound it' },
          offline_test: { type: 'string', description: 'a free replay assertion that must pass before any spend' },
        },
      },
    },
    rejected: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' }, description: 'defect + the measurement that kills it' },
  },
}

const plan = await agent(`${GROUND}

You have four independent forensic reads of the Opus cells. Reconcile them.

${valid.map((f, n) => `--- LENS ${LENSES[n]?.key || n} ---\nHEADLINE: ${f.headline}\nNUMBERS:\n${f.numbers}\nDEFECTS: ${JSON.stringify(f.defects)}`).join('\n\n')}

Rank every candidate defect by measured impact, not plausibility. REJECT any whose evidence is a
sub-bucket smaller than ~8 instances, or that contradicts the ground truth above, or that is a prompt
change. Accept AT MOST 3, each independently implementable and each with a free offline test that
would falsify it before any model spend.

Hard constraint: Haiku currently saves 25.0% and must not regress. For each accepted change state how
it could hurt Haiku and how that is bounded.

Be willing to conclude that 25% is not reachable on Opus by tool-side changes and to say what WOULD be
required instead. A defensible negative beats an invented positive.`,
  { label: 'synthesise', phase: 'Synthesise', schema: PLAN, effort: 'high' })

if (!plan || !plan.accepted || plan.accepted.length === 0) {
  return { verdict: plan?.verdict || 'no plan produced', rejected: plan?.rejected || [], implemented: [] }
}

phase('Implement')
const built = await pipeline(
  plan.accepted.slice(0, 3),
  (item, _orig, idx) => agent(`${GROUND}

Repo: ${REPO}. Create/checkout branch ${args.branch} (from the current HEAD; do NOT commit to main).
Work in your own git worktree so you cannot collide with the other implementers.

IMPLEMENT EXACTLY THIS ONE CHANGE, nothing else:
  title:  ${item.title}
  file:   ${item.file}
  change: ${item.change}
  why:    ${item.why}
  haiku risk: ${item.risk_to_haiku}

Rules:
- Tool-side only. Do NOT touch any prompt text or anything under ${SUITE}/tools/.
- Match the surrounding code's style and comment density. This codebase documents WHY with the
  measurement that motivated it — do that, citing the numbers from 'why' above.
- Add a regression test AND mutation-verify it: confirm the test FAILS with your change reverted and
  PASSES with it. Report both outcomes. A test that passes either way is worthless.
- Run: cd ${REPO} && go build ./... && go test ./internal/sem/ ./internal/cli/ -count=1
- If the change turns out to be wrong or unimplementable, say so and revert. Do not force it.

Return: branch name, files changed, the test name, the mutation-check result, and the build/test status.`,
    { label: `impl:${idx + 1}`, phase: 'Implement', isolation: 'worktree' }),
)

phase('Verify')
const verdict = await agent(`${GROUND}

Three implementation attempts on branch ${args.branch} in ${REPO}:
${built.filter(Boolean).map((b, n) => `--- attempt ${n + 1} ---\n${b}`).join('\n\n')}

Adversarially verify. Assume each is wrong until the repo proves otherwise:
1. Inspect the actual diff on the branch. Does the code do what the report claims?
2. cd ${REPO} && go build ./... && go test ./... -count=1 — report the true counts.
3. Re-run each regression test with the change reverted; confirm it fails. If a test passes with the
   change reverted, that finding is NOT verified — say so.
4. FREE OFFLINE REPLAY, before any model spend: build the binary and re-issue the recorded queries in
   ${SUITE}/results/R30Oeg/eg/*/gq_calls.log against ${SUITE}/replay-wt/<iid>, with a SEPARATE
   --cache-dir per binary (the index cache is tree-keyed, not binary-keyed: reuse one dir and the
   second build silently returns the first's payloads). Compare old vs new: gold-file rank must not
   regress on any instance, and report exactly what changed in the payloads.
5. Do the same replay against the HAIKU cell ${args.haiku_ref[0]} and confirm no gold-rank regression
   there either. This is the do-no-harm gate.

Return a table: change | builds | tests | mutation-verified | gold-rank delta Opus | gold-rank delta
Haiku | SHIP or HOLD. Then one paragraph: on this evidence, what does Opus actually get, and is 25%
reachable? Say plainly if it is not.`,
  { label: 'verify', phase: 'Verify', effort: 'high' })

return { verdict: plan.verdict, accepted: plan.accepted.map(a => a.title), rejected: plan.rejected, implementation: built.filter(Boolean), verification: verdict }

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""LITERAL OCCURRENCES — fold the baseline's winning move into the payload.

WHY, measured. Classifying every identifier the eg arm still grepped for that the payload did not
contain, against the repository's own symbol index (n=250 over 30 Sonnet sessions):

    51.2%  not a symbol at all -- a literal, an error string, a rule code, an operator expression
    38.0%  a symbol elsewhere in the repo
    10.8%  a symbol in a file the payload already named

The largest bucket is the one the tool has no verb for. `search` ranks semantically and `def` matches
symbols; neither answers "where does this exact text occur". That question is the no-tool baseline's
single most effective move -- on apache/lucene-13170 it solved the whole issue in three calls, the
first being `grep -n "sentenceStarts.length / 2"` on a string quoted verbatim in the bug report, while
the graph arm took ten. Separately, of the baseline's pre-edit locate work the payload answers 65% of
the READs but only 14% of the greps, and grep elimination is the strongest single predictor of whether
the tool saves money (corr +0.699 Sonnet, +0.615 Haiku).

WHAT IT EMITS. One block, occurrences only, no source bodies: `path:line` for each hit of each
distinctive literal drawn from the agent's own query. Bounded hard, because this is a navigation aid
and not reading material.

SELECTION. A literal qualifies only if it is distinctive enough to be a concept name rather than a
lexical magnet: it must contain a non-word character (`sentenceStarts.length / 2`, `__eq__`) or be an
ALL-CAPS/code-shaped token (`SIM201`), it must not be a plain English word, and its repository-wide
count must be small enough to enumerate. A literal occurring everywhere is not a locator, so it is
dropped rather than truncated -- a partial census reads as a complete one and is worse than silence.

Env: EG_LITERALS=<max occurrence lines, 0/unset = off>, WT (worktree), EG_LIT_QUERY (the query text).
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys

MAX = int(os.environ.get('EG_LITERALS', '0') or 0)
WT = os.environ.get('WT', '')
QUERY = os.environ.get('EG_LIT_QUERY', '')
MAX_PER_LIT = int(os.environ.get('EG_LIT_PER', '6') or 6)
STOP = set('''the a an and or of to in is are was were be been being this that these those with without
for from into onto over under after before while when where which what who whom whose how why not no
yes but if then else than as at by on off out up down all any some each every both few more most other
same such only own too very can will just should now does did doing done have has had having'''.split())


def literals(query):
    """Distinctive, code-shaped fragments of the query — never plain prose words."""
    out, seen = [], set()
    # quoted fragments first: a bug report quoting code is the strongest possible signal
    for m in re.findall(r'[`"\']([^`"\']{3,60})[`"\']', query):
        if m not in seen:
            seen.add(m); out.append(m)
    for tok in re.findall(r'[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*(?:\.[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)+|'
                          r'[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]{3,}|__\w+__|[a-z]+_[a-z_]{2,}', query):
        if tok.lower() in STOP or tok in seen or len(tok) < 4:
            continue
        seen.add(tok); out.append(tok)
    return out[:6]


def occurrences(lit, wt):
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(['grep', '-rn', '--binary-files=without-match', '-F', lit, wt],
                           capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=20)
    except Exception:
        return None
    lines = [l for l in r.stdout.splitlines() if l.strip()]
    if not lines or len(lines) > 40:
        return None            # a lexical magnet is not a locator; silence beats a partial census
    out = []
    for l in lines:
        parts = l.split(':', 2)
        if len(parts) < 3:
            continue
        p = parts[0][len(wt):].lstrip('/')
        if re.search(r'(^|/)(vendor|node_modules|third_party|dist|build|\.git)/', p):
            continue
        out.append((p, parts[1], parts[2].strip()[:90]))
    return out or None


def main():
    text = sys.stdin.read()
    if MAX <= 0 or not WT or not QUERY:
        sys.stdout.write(text); return
    blocks, used = [], 0
    for lit in literals(QUERY):
        if used >= MAX:
            break
        hits = occurrences(lit, WT)
        if not hits:
            continue
        shown = hits[:MAX_PER_LIT]
        used += len(shown)
        blocks.append('  "%s" — %d in %d files:' % (lit, len(hits), len({h[0] for h in hits})))
        for p, ln, src in shown:
            blocks.append('    %s:%s  %s' % (p, ln, src))
        if len(hits) > len(shown):
            blocks.append('    (+%d more)' % (len(hits) - len(shown)))
    if not blocks:
        sys.stdout.write(text); return
    sys.stdout.write(text.rstrip('\n') + '\n\nLITERAL OCCURRENCES (exact text from your query — this is your grep, already run):\n'
                     + '\n'.join(blocks) + '\n')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

```

- **pre-edit locate: v13 already cuts it 35%** (5.70 → 3.73). The payload works here.
- **post-edit locate: grows** (3.00 → 3.97). A turn-1 payload cannot reach this by construction.

So 33% was never available from a static payload. What *is* available is closing the post-edit gap — worth roughly 1.0–1.5 calls/session, and if it also stops the pre-edit win leaking back, Sonnet lands somewhere in the low teens negative rather than −2.2%. 1	# entire-graph: accuracy + token/latency losses from corpus pollution, no index reuse, and non-score ranking
2	
3	**Type:** bug / performance
4	**Area:** `entire graph search` · `impact` · index/preselection
5	**Severity:** high — the two symptoms an agent notices first are *"the top hit points at a file that isn't the real one"* (trust) and *"one query reads tens of MB and takes 13–30 s"* (tokens/latency). Both are traced to concrete, fixable root causes below.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## TL;DR
10	
11	Dogfooded the graph on **its own repo** (query: *"how are semantic search hits ranked and scored"*), measured a **clean checkout (146 Go source files, tracked)** against the **working tree as it sits on disk (with `.claude/worktrees/`)**. Findings, most-leverage first:
12	
13	| # | Finding | Hurts | Measured |
14	|---|---------|-------|----------|
15	| **T1** | **Generated tree-sitter grammar blobs are indexed** (`internal/sem/grammars/*/parser.c`) — **tracked in the repo, so every clone hits this** | tokens, accuracy | 11 `parser.c`, **193 MB**; julia alone **53 MB**; ~52 MB read on a 146-file repo; they fail to parse → completeness downgraded to `degraded` |
16	| **T2** | **`.claude/worktrees/` agent scratch is indexed** — untracked, not gitignored | trust, tokens, latency | 1.5 GB, 1044 `.go` copies; corpus **146 → 2585 files scanned**; **8 / 10 top hits point at throwaway worktree copies**; `impact` **hung > 2 min**; 76 MB read; 30 s |
17	| **T3** | **Index is rebuilt on every invocation** (`index_cache_hit: false` / `cache-miss` every call) | tokens, latency | search **13 s**, impact **31 s** on the *same unchanged* clean tree — back-to-back calls both paid full build |
18	| **A1** | **Final ordering is not sorted by score** | trust | rank 7 (`SearchRepository`, 19.8) outscores ranks 3–6 (17.6/17.1/16.6/16.4); rank 10 has **score 0** and no symbol name |
19	| **A2** | **Context budget spent on duplicate / zero-value snippets** | tokens | 6–8 of 10 snippets truncated by budget; worktree-duplicate full bodies eat the budget canonical hits need |
20	| **A3** | **`type_card` surfaces trivial locals** (earlier run: `minimal`/`compact`/`rich` string vars) instead of meaningful types | accuracy | noise bytes per query |
21	
22	**One-line fix priority:** exclude generated-parser blobs + agent worktrees from the corpus, reuse the built index across invocations, and sort output by score. T1+T2+T3 together take a query from *52–76 MB / 13–30 s / 8-of-10-wrong* to roughly *~2 MB / <2 s / canonical hits*.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## How this was measured
27	
28	- **Clean tree:** `git archive HEAD | tar -x` of `entire-graph` → **146 `.go` files**, no `.claude/worktrees/`. Fresh `git init/add/commit` so the graph sees a normal repo.
29	- **Polluted tree:** the working directory as it actually sits (what an agent's `--repo .` sees), which contains `.claude/worktrees/agent-*/…` from prior agent runs.
30	- Same query on both, `--profile full --format json`, stats block captured verbatim. `impact` timed separately.
31	- Nothing was fetched, pulled, or deleted from the repo; the clean tree is a throwaway copy.
32	
33	---
34	
35	## Accuracy / trustworthiness
36	
37	### A0 (root cause of the "not trustworthy" feeling) — worktree copies win the ranking
38	On the **polluted** tree, **8 of the top 10 hits pointed at `.claude/worktrees/agent-XXXXX/internal/sem/…`** — stale duplicate copies — instead of the canonical `internal/sem/*.go`. An agent told by the doctrine to *"edit the top hit directly from search output"* edits a throwaway tree; the change lands nowhere and the build is unaffected. This is the single biggest trust failure and it is invisible unless you notice the path prefix.
39	
40	On the **clean** tree the exact same query returns **0 worktree hits** — every hit is canonical (`internal/cli/search.go`, `internal/sem/search*.go`). So the tool is *correct* on a clean corpus and *untrustworthy* only because it indexes scratch trees. Fix = stop indexing them (see F-fixes).
41	
42	### A1 — final order is not score order
43	Clean-tree top 10 (rank | score | symbol):
44	
45	```
46	 1 | 23.686 | agentSearchLocationHeaders   internal/cli/search.go:641
47	 2 | 21.317 | agentSearchBlock             internal/cli/search.go:611
48	 3 | 17.635 | loadOrBuildSearchGraphSnapshot
49	 4 | 17.056 | dedupeSemanticMirrorCandidates
50	 5 | 16.553 | mergeSearchRelatedSites
51	 6 | 16.447 | countBudgetTruncatedResults
52	 7 | 19.806 | SearchRepository             internal/sem/search.go:662   ← outscores 3–6
53	 8 | 15.314 | AssessSearchConfidence
54	 9 | 14.119 | assignSearchSections
55	10 |  0.000 | (no symbol name)            internal/sem/search_mirror_dedup.go:153
56	```
57	
58	`SearchRepository` — arguably *the* answer to "how are hits ranked" — is buried at **rank 7** despite scoring higher than the four hits above it, and a **score-0, unnamed fragment** occupies rank 10. The doctrine promises "the top hit is the fix site"; when rank and score disagree, agents that trust rank 1–3 and stop are steered wrong. **Fix:** sort emitted hits by score (or, if a deliberate re-rank exists, emit the effective score you sorted on so rank is explainable).
59	
60	### A2 — score-0 / unnamed fragments occupy top-10 slots
61	Rank 10 above has score 0 and no `symbol_name` — a non-actionable fragment taking a slot a real candidate could use. **Fix:** drop score-0 and un-symboled fragments from the ranked list (or floor the list at a minimum score).
62	
63	### A3 — `type_card` surfaces trivial locals
64	An earlier run's `type_card` listed local string vars (`minimal`, `compact`, `rich`) rather than meaningful types for the query — pure noise bytes. **Fix:** exclude function-local declarations from `type_card`; prefer package-level types referenced by the top hits.
65	
66	### A4 — mirror-dedup doesn't cover worktrees
67	`dedupeSemanticMirrorCandidates` exists to collapse mirror paths but did **not** collapse the `.claude/worktrees/` duplicates of the same symbols. Even once worktrees are excluded from indexing, the dedup fingerprint should treat *same qualified-name, different worktree root* as a duplicate as a defense-in-depth.
68	
69	---
70	
71	## Token savings (the big lever)
72	
73	### T1 — generated grammar `parser.c` is indexed (in-repo, affects every clone)
74	`internal/sem/grammars/` is **193 MB** of vendored, machine-generated tree-sitter parsers — **11 `parser.c` files, all tracked**:
75	
76	```
77	 53.4 MB  internal/sem/grammars/julia/parser.c
78	 31.2 MB  internal/sem/grammars/fsharp/parser.c
79	 28.9 MB  internal/sem/grammars/csharp/parser.c
80	 28.4 MB  internal/sem/grammars/objc/parser.c
81	 19.6 MB  internal/sem/grammars/perl/parser.c
82	 … (sum of grammar *.c/*.json = 192.9 MB)
83	git check-ignore → NOT-IGNORED    git ls-files parser.c → 11 (tracked)
84	```
85	
86	This is why a query on a **146-file repo reads 52 MB**: the graph opens these generated blobs, fails to parse them (`partial E_PARSE_ERROR: internal/sem/grammars/clojure/parser.c`), and reports **`Completeness: degraded (262/272 files parsed; 13 partial failures)`**. Because they're *tracked*, this hits every user of entire-graph on this repo, not just this machine — so it's the most universal token drain here.
87	
88	**Fix:** exclude generated/vendored parser sources from indexing. Options: (a) a built-in skip rule for `**/grammars/**/parser.c` + `parser.h` + generated `grammar.json`/`node-types.json`; (b) more generally, skip files above a size threshold (e.g. 1–2 MB) and files matching generated-artifact heuristics; (c) respect a `.graphignore`. A 53 MB single-file read for a Go-repo query is never intended.
89	
90	### T2 — `.claude/worktrees/` agent scratch is indexed
91	Untracked, **not gitignored**, **1.5 GB, 1044 `.go` copies**. Effect on the same query:
92	
93	| metric | clean (146 files) | polluted (worktrees present) |
94	|---|---|---|
95	| files scanned | 317 | **2585** |
96	| bytes read / query | 52.5 MB | **76.2 MB** |
97	| search latency | 13.2 s | **29.9 s** |
98	| `impact` | 31 s (completes) | **> 2 min → timeout/kill** |
99	| top-10 hits on canonical paths | 10 / 10 | **2 / 10** |
100	
101	Worktrees turn `impact` — the one-shot blast-radius command the doctrine tells agents to trust — into a >2 min hang, which forces the exact grep fallback the graph exists to prevent. **Fix:** defensively skip nested git worktrees / known agent-scratch roots (`.claude/worktrees/`, `.worktrees/`, `.entire/`) from indexing and preselection **even when not gitignored** — a nested worktree is by definition a duplicate of tracked content and should never be a fix site. (Belt-and-suspenders: the repo could also add `.claude/worktrees/` to `.gitignore`, but the tool shouldn't depend on that.)
102	
103	### T3 — the index is rebuilt on every invocation
104	Both commands, run back-to-back on the **same unchanged clean tree**, reported a full rebuild:
105	
106	```
107	search:  index_cache_hit: false   total_latency_ms: 13154
108	impact:  Index: cache-miss (31195ms) | Query: 5ms | Total: 31201ms
109	```
110	
111	The *query* itself is 5 ms; **~100 % of wall-clock is index build**, paid again every call. For an agent doing locate → impact → verify, that's three full rebuilds per task. This is the highest-leverage latency fix after excluding the pollution that inflates each build. **Fix:** persist and reuse the built index keyed by tree state (content digest / mtime set), invalidating only changed files; a warm cache should take these to sub-second query time.
112	
113	### T4 — context budget spent on duplicates and fragments
114	6–8 of 10 snippets were truncated by the 24 KB context budget. On the polluted tree, full-body worktree *duplicates* (e.g. ranks 2 and 5) consumed budget that canonical hits then couldn't get, so real hits came back truncated to fragments that force a file open — a second token hit. Fixing T1/T2/A2 reclaims that budget for the hits that matter.
115	
116	---
117	
118	## Recommended fixes, ranked by leverage
119	
120	1. **Exclude generated/vendored parser blobs from the corpus** (T1) — skip `**/grammars/**/parser.{c,h}` + generated grammar JSON, and/or a size cap (≥1–2 MB) + generated-artifact heuristic. *Universal win: −~50 MB/query, fixes `degraded` completeness, affects every clone.*
121	2. **Skip nested worktrees / agent-scratch roots even when un-ignored** (T2, A0, A4) — `.claude/worktrees/`, `.worktrees/`, `.entire/`. *Restores hit trust (2/10 → 10/10 canonical), 2585 → ~317 files, un-hangs `impact`.*
122	3. **Persist and reuse the index across invocations** (T3) — key on tree digest, invalidate per changed file. *13–31 s → sub-second on warm cache.*
123	4. **Sort emitted hits by score; drop score-0/unnamed fragments** (A1, A2) — or emit the effective re-rank score so rank is explainable. *Restores the "trust the top hit" contract.*
124	5. **Exclude function-local decls from `type_card`** (A3). *Removes per-query noise.*
125	
126	---
127	
128	## Appendix — raw stats
129	
130	**Clean (146 tracked Go files, no worktrees):**
131	`files_scanned: 317 · bytes_read: 52,520,473 · latency: 13,154 ms · index_cache_hit: false · truncated_by_budget: 8 · complete_symbol_snippets: 5 · worktree hits: 0/10 · impact: 31,201 ms (completes)`
132	
133	**Polluted (working tree with `.claude/worktrees/`):**
134	`files_scanned: 2585 · bytes_read: 76,177,194 · latency: 29,900 ms · truncated_by_budget: 6 · complete_symbol_snippets: 5 · worktree hits: 8/10 · impact/explain: >120 s → killed`
135	
136	**Pollution inventory:**
137	`grammars: 193 MB, 11 tracked parser.c (julia 53 MB) — NOT gitignored`
138	`.claude/worktrees/: 1.5 GB, 1044 .go copies, untracked — NOT gitignored`
139	
140	**Completeness signal (clean tree):** `degraded (262/272 files parsed; 1 warning; 13 partial failures)` — the 13 failures are the generated grammar sources.
141	
142	*Method note: measured by diffing a `git archive HEAD` clean checkout against the on-disk working tree; no fetch/pull/reset performed against the live repo.*

Zero score-0 hits in **178 benchmark payloads** — A2 is specific to that one entire-graph query, not general.

**Final verdict on the ISSUE, all measured rather than assumed:**

- **T1, T2 — already fixed in HEAD.** The Opus agent measured a stale binary. Current HEAD reads 2.8 MB not 52 MB and returns 0 scratch hits despite 2.2 GB of un-ignored worktrees sitting right there.
- **T3 — CONFIRMED and it's the one that matters for all agents.** `index_cache_hit=False` on the *second identical call*; 8876 ms of the 9297 ms total is index build, paid **every single invocation**. On a large repo that's the 13–31 s the ISSUE reports. That's real waste, though it's latency rather than tokens.
- **A1 — real (27.4% of payloads) but the proposed fix is wrong.** I tested it: score-sorting moves gold@1 by +2 and gold@3 by **−2**, and the gap's miss-prediction AUC gets *worse* (0.542 → 0.523). The re-rank is deliberate and slightly better than score order. The right fix is the ISSUE's own alternative — emit the effective score so rank is explainable — not re-sorting.
- **A2 — real on that repo, 0/178 in benchmark payloads.**

So: **none of these explain the Sonnet losses.** T3 is genuinely worth fixing for every agent using the tool, and it's the strongest item in that report.

One thing it did change for me: A1 meant my confidence tier computes its gap from a mis-ordered list. I re-tested and the tier still stands (score-sorting wouldn't improve it), but that was worth knowing rather than assuming.

**Goal status unchanged and honest:** Haiku **−25.0%** [−32.2, −17.0] met; Sonnet best-ever **−2.2%** suite / **−23.4%** exploration-heavy, tier verified safe on Haiku (+0.7%); Opus workflow still running. v15 escalation is at 12/30 on Sonnet — that's the remaining live shot at the post-edit gap, which is where I traced the last of the loss.

Deliberately **excluded**: the unmeasured constant-extraction work (stashed), and the confidence tier — that one lives in the benchmark wrapper because it's a caller policy (how many hits to request), not a tool default. baseline post-edit locate: 3.50 calls  <- a turn-1 payload cannot, by construction

33% needs the payload to fully substitute pre-edit locate. content.text:
**Sonnet's full potential, decomposed from the measured phase split** (19.07 baseline tool calls/session):

| scenario | calls | vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| baseline (no tool) | 19.07 | 0.0% |
| **eg v13 today** | 19.77 | +3.7% |
| **A** — zero exploration ever (physically impossible) | 8.27 | −56.6% |
| **B** — perfect turn-1 payload, post-edit untouched | 11.77 | **−38.3%** |
| **C** — payload answers 90% of reads + 43% of greps | 15.28 | −19.9% |
| **D** — C + post-edit stops growing | 13.84 | **−27.4%** |
| **E** — D + eg batches probes like the baseline | 12.03 | −36.9% |

**B (−38.3%) is the hard ceiling** for anything delivered at turn 1 — post-edit locate is unreachable by construction. **25% sits inside the attainable band**, which is the direct answer to your question.

Worth in points:
```
payload answers the reads it can      -23.6 pt
stop the post-edit give-back           -7.6 pt   <- v15 escalation targets this
batch residual shell probes            -9.5 pt
```

**Three caveats, because this is arithmetic and not a promise:**

1. **Arithmetic ≠ mechanism.** Scenario C assumes the payload answers 43% of pre-edit greps — that's the *symbol-ish* fraction, an upper bound on what's answerable. Every expansion I actually tested reaches ≤11%. So of the −23.6 pt in that row, I have a demonstrated mechanism for maybe a quarter.
2. **Calls aren't cost.** v13 is **+3.7% in calls but −2.2% in USD** — it makes slightly more calls, each cheaper. So this table is a good structural guide and a poor cost predictor; the two diverge by ~6 points on the one config where I have both.
3. **Batching (−9.5 pt) has no mechanism at all.** eg's arm gets the same "batch your probes" instruction as the baseline and batches less (1.42 vs 2.00 probes/call). I don't know why, and prompt changes have backfired three times.

**So the honest split:** arithmetic potential −27% to −37%; mechanism-backed potential today is roughly **−10% to −15%** (v13's tier, plus escalation if v15 confirms, plus FILE OUTLINE at ~5%). The gap between those two numbers is the real remaining work, and the biggest single unknown in it is why Sonnet fragments its shell calls.
